findings.description: Generic OpenWrt 6.12 config has eBPF syscall and JIT enabled but NOT the networking pieces needed for TC/XDP-socket use; everything else is a kmod or build option.
findings.technical_details: CONFIG_BPF=y, BPF_JIT=y, BPF_JIT_DEFAULT_ON=y, BPF_SYSCALL=y, BPF_UNPRIV_DEFAULT_OFF=y (root only), BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON not set, BPF_STREAM_PARSER not set, DEBUG_INFO_BTF not set, NET_CLS_ACT/NET_SCH_INGRESS/NET_CLS_BPF/NET_ACT_BPF not set (kmod-sched-bpf, kmod-sched-core provide them as modules via KCONFIG in netsupport.mk), XDP_SOCKETS not set, NET_SOCK_MSG=y, CGROUPS not set at generic level, NF_FLOW_TABLE not set (kmod), NF_TPROXY/NFT_TPROXY/NFT_SOCKET not set (kmods). Per-target configs may change CGROUPS (procd option), unverified for per-target.

findings.topic: Which BPF program types need which config
findings.description: sockmap/sockhash + sk_skb stream_verdict + sk_msg only need BPF_SYSCALL (which selects NET_SOCK_MSG); BPF_STREAM_PARSER (stream_parser, needs CGROUP_BPF) is NOT needed for stream_verdict. sk_lookup needs BPF_SYSCALL only. TC-BPF needs NET_CLS_BPF/NET_ACT_BPF/NET_SCH_INGRESS/NET_SCH_CLSACT modules. cgroup/connect4/6 needs CGROUPS+CGROUP_BPF and cgroup2 mount (not guaranteed on OpenWrt). XDP generic needs only BPF_SYSCALL; native needs driver ndo_bpf.
findings.technical_details: So sockmap is the one eBPF feature that works on the stock OpenWrt kernel without extra kmods. cgroup hooks are the most config-fragile (mihomo already runs outside any special cgroup; connect hooks could not distinguish mihomo's own sockets without cgroup membership).
findings.opus_note: openwrt:config-6.12 NET_SOCK_MSG=y, BPF_SYSCALL=y builds sock_map.o (linux:net/core/Makefile:42-43); verdict-only path sk_psock_start_verdict (skmsg.c:1306) is outside the BPF_STREAM_PARSER block (1113-1239). Resolves the conflict with openwrt_kernel F004/F021.

findings.topic: XDP: driver support on router SoCs
findings.description: XDP is a poor fit: it sees only raw frames before the stack, cannot terminate or redirect to a local userspace socket, and cannot skip mihomo for classified traffic better than flowtable does. mtk_eth_soc exposes native XDP (BASIC|REDIRECT|NDO_XMIT) but only when page_pool is enabled; ndo_bpf=mtk_xdp. mt7621 (ramips) PAGE_POOL is set in config. Many wifi/switch ports (DSA user ports, mt76 WLAN) have no native XDP, generic XDP (skb-mode) runs after skb alloc with little gain.
findings.technical_details: mtk_eth_soc xdp_features set at 4820-4823 only if mtk_page_pool_enabled(). XDP and the hardware flow offload (PPE) of Filogic overlap: PPE offload (via flowtable HW offload) already bypasses the CPU entirely, which XDP cannot match. XDP cannot be used on bridged WLAN clients. XDP is IPv4/IPv6 and TCP/UDP capable but sees no conntrack state unless it uses bpf_skb/xdp conntrack kfuncs (bpf_xdp_ct_lookup, needs NF_CONNTRACK + kfunc support, hypothesis for 6.12 config on OpenWrt).

findings.description: TC-BPF at ingress/egress can run on any netdev (incl. bridge ports, WLAN) with skb context, can read ct state via bpf_skb_ct_lookup kfunc (hypothesis re: availability) and can do bpf_sk_assign (TPROXY-like steering) and mark/redirect. But it only needs to exist if nftables sets can't express the policy; nftables already handles IP/CIDR set lookups natively and fw4 owns the ruleset.
findings.technical_details: Needs kmod-sched-core + kmod-sched-bpf (NET_CLS_ACT, NET_SCH_INGRESS, NET_CLS_BPF, NET_ACT_BPF) which are NOT built-in in the generic config (+~100-200 KB modules, size unverified). cilium/ebpf supports TCX (kernel >=6.6, link/tcx.go) which fits 6.12; older kernels need netlink clsact qdisc setup. bpf_sk_assign and bpf_skb_set_tunnel_key exist in filter.c.

findings.topic: sockmap redirect for terminated DIRECT connections: mechanism
findings.description: A sockhash holding the client socket and upstream socket, with an sk_skb stream_verdict program doing bpf_sk_redirect_hash(skb,&map,&key,0) (egress) on each, moves payload between two ESTABLISHED TCP sockets in-kernel without userspace copying. Constraints are strict: only ESTABLISHED sockets for redirect, listen sockets excluded for redirect.
findings.technical_details: sock_map_redirect_allowed: TCP requires state != TCP_LISTEN; sock_map_sk_state_allowed: ESTABLISHED or LISTEN for TCP, hashed UDP, unix stream, vsock. TCP data path: sk_psock_verdict_data_ready calls ops->read_skb (tcp_read_skb) which unlinks skbs from sk_receive_queue and passes each to sk_psock_verdict_recv -> BPF verdict -> sk_psock_skb_redirect to peer's egress queue, sent by a workqueue (sk_psock_backlog), not in softirq context. IPv6 sockets are supported (tcpv6 prot rebuilt, tcp_bpf.c:622-654). UDP only via skb_verdict, not meaningful for QUIC/ DIRECT UDP proxies.

findings.topic: sockmap limitations for a proxy (half-close, RST, accounting, ordering)
findings.description: Proxy semantics are not fully preserved: (a) FIN/RST are not translated into shutdown/close on the peer; tcp_read_skb stops at an skb with FIN and the verdict program only sees a zero-length skb, so userspace must detect EOF out of band (e.g. poll for EPOLLRDHUP on the sockmap'd socket, still delivered via data_ready? hypothesis) and then call shutdown(peer, SHUT_WR); (b) bytes already sitting in sk_receive_queue before insertion (e.g. data mihomo peeked for TLS SNI sniffing and the unread remainder) stay in the receive queue of the old socket and are not redirected, so userspace must drain/forward them first and only then insert into the map (ordering race with new arrivals); (c) socket buffer accounting: redirected skbs are charged to the receiving psock and the egress socket's sndbuf; slow peers can cause backlog growth bounded by sk_psock ingress queue / sk_rcvbuf; (d) after insertion userspace read() on the fd goes through tcp_bpf_recvmsg_parser/ tcp_bpf_recvmsg - not for proxies reading bytes, so Go's netpoll semantics change; (e) errors on peer produce sk_err on the other socket asynchronously.
findings.technical_details: Hence a robust design needs a userspace supervisor goroutine per connection (or a conn-level epoll) anyway, which weakens the memory benefit: Go goroutine stack per connection (~2-8 KB) remains plus fds. Idle-timeout, traffic accounting (up/down bytes for the dashboard), and rate limiting / connection statistics are lost unless read from tcp_info (TCP_INFO bytes_received/bytes_acked are available) or sockmap-side counters in a BPF map. This breaks mihomo's per-connection statistics hooks unless re-implemented through tcp_info polling.

findings.topic: Go TCPConn.ReadFrom already uses splice(2) between two TCP sockets
findings.description: Go (1.27.3 stdlib here) io.Copy(dstTCP, srcTCP) takes TCPConn.readFrom -> spliceFrom: if the reader is a *TCPConn (or tcpConnWithoutWriteTo) or a unix stream conn, it splices kernel-side through a pipe (socket->pipe->socket), no userspace copy. Optionally LimitedReader supported. spliceTo (WriteTo path) is only enabled when dst is a stream UnixConn. This works only if mihomo's relay passes the bare *net.TCPConn objects (not wrapped by statistic tracker, buffered reader, or TLS), which is true for the DIRECT/TPROXY path only when no wrapper intervenes.
findings.technical_details: This is the baseline non-BPF alternative: kernel does the copy, but two syscalls-per-chunk wake-ups (splice in + splice out, up to pipe size 64 KB default) per direction occur in userspace and each readiness wake-up goes through the Go netpoller; CPU cost on MT7621-class cores is dominated by the Go scheduler wake-ups plus kernel copy via the pipe (page refs, not memcpy for TCP->pipe on splice from socket: it does copy from skb frags into pipe pages for many drivers). mihomo's tunnel/relay in the fork still needs checking whether it uses the bare TCPConn (see opportunities).
findings.opus_note: True for Go stdlib, but mihomo's relay uses sing's own splice (mod:sing@v0.5.8/common/bufio/splice_linux.go) via copyDirect, not net.TCPConn.ReadFrom.

findings.description: No measured numbers exist for these hardware targets in this study. Hypothesis: sockmap redirect removes the userspace wake-ups and syscalls entirely (data_ready -> BPF -> backlog worker), so it would cut CPU per byte versus splice mostly by removing per-chunk syscalls and context switches, but both still traverse the full TCP stack twice (rx + tx), so the gain over splice is bounded (guess: tens of percent CPU at best), while the gain over a plain userspace io.Copy with 16-32 KB buffers (two memcpys + 2 syscalls/chunk) is larger. Hardware flowtable/PPE offload on a pure forwarding path beats both.
findings.technical_details: Known public data points (secondary): Cloudflare/Cilium sockmap-accelerated proxying reports gains on x86 servers; no MIPS/ARMv7 data. Treat as hypothesis. Recommended measurement: iperf3 through a TPROXY'd DIRECT flow on a MT7621 / filogic device comparing (a) io.Copy w/ buffer, (b) splice (Go default), (c) sockmap, measuring CPU idle% and throughput.

findings.description: sk_lookup (BPF_SK_LOOKUP, netns-attached link) lets a BPF program choose the listening socket for incoming connections/datagrams (bpf_sk_assign) based on dest IP/port, but it only acts on traffic destined to local addresses; it cannot capture forwarded LAN traffic (dst not local) the way TPROXY with policy routing / local route does. For a router intercepting forwarded flows you still need nft tproxy / REDIRECT or a TUN. A tc-bpf program using bpf_sk_assign can capture non-local dst, like TPROXY, replacing nft tproxy but not simpler.
findings.technical_details: So sk_lookup is useful for steering many ports to one listener (e.g. 'all ports' without a port range DNAT) after traffic is already delivered locally (e.g. via ip rule local route). Not a net win vs nft tproxy which fw4 already supports. Supported TCP and UDP, IPv4/IPv6 (kernel >=5.9). Config: BPF_SYSCALL only; attach via link (cilium/ebpf link.AttachNetNs).

findings.topic: Bypass of not-yet-intercepted traffic: eBPF map vs nft set + flowtable
findings.description: For forwarded traffic the existing mechanism (nft set of classified DIRECT destinations consulted before the tproxy rule, plus flowtable software/hardware offload for established flows) gives the same bypass with kernel-supported, fw4-integrated pieces. An XDP/TC program with a hash map filled by mihomo could bypass the tproxy decision earlier but still needs a way to also skip nft hooks/conntrack, which XDP_PASS does not do; only XDP_REDIRECT-style forwarding does and it bypasses the firewall (safety problem). nft set+flowtable is simpler and safer: atomic transactions, timeouts per element, interval sets for CIDR, fw4 reload keeps ruleset consistent, auto-flush on mihomo exit via the set living in fw4/tables.
findings.technical_details: eBPF map advantages: LRU eviction, per-element stats, wide key types (5-tuple instead of dst-only). Disadvantages: needs kmod-sched-bpf, no FW4 awareness, map lifetime must be pinned, leak risk if mihomo crashes while program stays attached (stale 'bypass' = traffic leaking around the proxy), verifier/JIT variance across the 5 architectures. The clashwrt setctl.sh/fw.sh already implements an nft bypass set; see consumer project.

findings.topic: BPF JIT availability per architecture (OpenWrt targets)
findings.description: eBPF JIT exists for all OpenWrt arches in v6.12: arm64 (HAVE_EBPF_JIT), arm 32-bit ARMv7 (HAVE_EBPF_JIT if !CPU_ENDIAN_BE32 && !CPU_32v3), MIPS (32 and 64: bpf_jit_comp32.c / comp64.c, except microMIPS), riscv (MMU only). MIPS eBPF JIT (32-bit variant by Johan Almbladh) merged around Linux 5.16 (from memory; unverified).
findings.technical_details: Without JIT, eBPF is interpreted; OpenWrt sets BPF_JIT_DEFAULT_ON=y and not ALWAYS_ON, so the interpreter fallback is enabled if the JIT is disabled via sysctl net.core.bpf_jit_enable=0. Interpreter is several times slower; for sockmap verdict programs per-skb cost is small anyway, but for per-packet TC/XDP on MT7621 it matters. big-endian ARM (CPU_ENDIAN_BE32) has no JIT; ath79/ramips big-endian MIPS is covered. MIPS 32-bit with 64-bit atomics/bpf_loop etc. has restricted insns support.
findings.opus_note: linux:arch/mips/net/bpf_jit_comp32.c and bpf_jit_comp64.c, arch/arm/net/bpf_jit_32.c exist in 6.12.112

findings.topic: BTF/CO-RE not available on OpenWrt kernels
findings.description: CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF is unset, so /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux does not exist; CO-RE relocations and fentry/kprobe-with-struct-access programs cannot be portably loaded. Network-type programs (sk_skb, sk_msg, sk_lookup, xdp, tc) that only use their stable UAPI contexts (__sk_buff, sk_msg_md, bpf_sk_lookup, xdp_md) need no BTF and no CO-RE, so they can be built once per arch with clang -target bpf and embedded as ELF via bpf2go.
findings.technical_details: bpf2go needs clang at dev time only. Maps declared in legacy or BTF-style: BTF-defined maps (.maps section) require the program ELF's own BTF (compiler-generated, fine) but the loader also strips/does not need vmlinux BTF; cilium/ebpf handles missing kernel BTF unless CO-RE relocations or typed kfunc calls are present. Verifier limits on 6.12: 1M insn complexity, bounded loops allowed; older kernels (<5.2) no bounded loops; irrelevant for 6.12 but matters for OpenWrt 23.05 (5.15) and 22.03 (5.10) — sockmap stream_verdict first appears in 5.13, sk_lookup 5.9, TCX 6.6.

findings.topic: cilium/ebpf: pure Go, no libbpf; supports sockmap, XDP, TCX, netns/sk_lookup, cgroup
findings.description: cilium/ebpf (go 1.26.0, repo at commit 7963e20, 2026-10-29) is pure Go with no cgo; supports map types incl. SockMap/SockHash, program types SkSKB/SkMsg/SkLookup/XDP/SchedCLS, links for XDP, TCX, netns, cgroup, and pinning of maps/programs/links in bpffs. Requires golang.org/x/sys (already a mihomo dependency) and uses the kernel's BPF syscall directly.
findings.technical_details: Package list pulled by a minimal sockmap program: github.com/cilium/ebpf, /asm, /btf, /internal/{sys,unix,linux,platform,kallsyms,kconfig,tracefs,mountinfo,sysenc} and golang.org/x/sys/unix, plus std reflect, encoding/binary, os (the others, crypto etc., come from fmt/os in the test program). Link pinning: RawLink.Pin / Unpin in link/link.go:164-173; program/map pinning via pin package.

findings.topic: Experiment: binary size cost of importing cilium/ebpf (stripped, -ldflags -s -w -trimpath, CGO off, Go 1.27.3)
findings.description: A minimal program that creates a SockHash map and loads an SkSKB program with cilium/ebpf adds about 1.64 MB on arm64 (1,573,024 -> 3,211,424 bytes; hello-world baseline), 1.70 MB on arm32 (same ending size, ~3.2 MB, baseline 1,507,488), and 1.97 MB on mipsle softfloat (1,704,127 -> 3,670,207). This is a standalone overstatement: mihomo already links reflect, encoding/binary, os, golang.org/x/sys/unix and fmt-era runtime, so the real delta inside mihomo is estimated at ~0.8-1.3 MB (hypothesis, not measured).
findings.technical_details: The big contributors are cilium/ebpf/btf (BTF parser/marshaler, kconfig and kallsyms) which cannot be eliminated by build tags; using only the sys package (github.com/cilium/ebpf/internal/sys is internal, not importable) isn't possible, so a leaner alternative is a tiny hand-written wrapper over golang.org/x/sys/unix.Syscall(SYS_BPF,...) for BPF_MAP_CREATE/BPF_PROG_LOAD/BPF_MAP_UPDATE_ELEM/BPF_PROG_ATTACH with a hand-assembled static program (~300 lines) that adds <50 KB. Source: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-mrfrok-Projects-clashwrt/0712caf5-593b-4903-aa33-590a1010ee6c/scratchpad/ebpf_xdp_research/ebpf/main.go and empty/main.go. Not run on a device: the host runtime test of loading wasn't executed to avoid touching host state; kernel-loaded behaviour unverified.

findings.description: BPF map/program creation needs CAP_BPF (kernel>=5.8) plus CAP_NET_ADMIN for network program types, and CAP_PERFMON for some; on OpenWrt mihomo already runs as root. Resources are fd-refcounted: if programs/maps are only held by mihomo's fds, they are freed when the process dies (safe: no stale bypass). Pinned objects in bpffs (needs mount -t bpf, CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL; OpenWrt does not mount bpffs by default, unverified) or link-attached objects (XDP/TCX/cgroup/netns links are destroyed with the last fd unless pinned) outlive the process. Legacy netlink attach (TC clsact filters, XDP via netlink without link) always outlives the process.
findings.technical_details: Safety rule for the bypass use-case: use non-pinned links so that crash/exit auto-detaches (fail-closed); never pin. Sockmaps: sockets removed from the map when closed; psock detaches on socket close; crash closes all sockets so connections die with the process (same as today).

findings.description: XDP runs before nf hooks and conntrack: packets handled in XDP never create conntrack entries and bypass fw4 rules entirely (firewall bypass risk). TC-BPF runs after ingress qdisc and before nf PREROUTING (ingress) / after POSTROUTING hooks on egress (clsact egress runs before netfilter egress hooks), also outside nft policy unless the program calls bpf_skb_ct_lookup. sockmap runs on socket layer, after nf and conntrack, so it composes with firewall policy and conntrack safely. Software flowtable (nf_flow_table) is the standard in-kernel fast path after conntrack and respects fw4 offload settings.
findings.technical_details: Hence of the eBPF options only sockmap composes with the existing firewall without bypass risk. For TPROXY traffic, mihomo's sockets are local (conntrack entry exists, tproxy assigned), which flowtable can never offload since it is locally terminated.

findings.description: sockmap handles UDP only as skb_verdict between hashed UDP sockets (sock_map_sk_state_allowed: sk_is_udp -> sk_hashed), without connection semantics; QUIC DIRECT flows in mihomo's UDP NAT proxy cannot be redirected between 'client' and 'upstream' as a stream; each UDP packet needs source address rewriting (userspace does that today). So UDP is not accelerated by sockmap in any useful way.
findings.technical_details: The only in-kernel UDP fast path is flowtable for forwarded (non-intercepted) flows, i.e. DIRECT UDP traffic that is NOT sent to mihomo at all (bypass by IP/port sets), which requires classification without domain data in practice.

findings.topic: TLS sniffing and DIRECT first bytes
findings.description: For a TPROXY'd DIRECT connection mihomo reads the first bytes (TLS ClientHello SNI) to classify, then dials upstream. After sniff, those bytes are already consumed by userspace and written to the upstream socket by write(); only the *rest* of the stream could be sockmap-offloaded. This makes the handoff point after the first request exactly once per connection: userspace sets the upstream socket and client socket into a sockhash (fd insert via BPF_MAP_UPDATE_ELEM) when both ESTABLISHED and both receive queues are drained; there is an inherent race for data arriving during the switch.
findings.technical_details: Quantitative scope: this only helps long-lived bulk DIRECT flows (downloads/video). Short HTTP flows pay the map-insert syscalls and psock allocation for no gain. A size threshold trigger (e.g. after N KB moved) is hypothesis for a hybrid policy.

findings.topic: Custom kernel module / TUN stack comparison
findings.description: A custom kernel module (e.g. a netfilter hook with a classified-flow table, or an ipt/nft expr) could do the same bypass as nft sets with fewer constraints but must be built per kernel version/arch ABI with every OpenWrt snapshot (vermagic, kmod packaging), and is a stability and security burden; nft sets/flowtable (in-tree, maintained by firewall4 and kmod-nft-offload) already cover the semantic. TC u32/flower can match prefix sets but have no dynamic set semantics, no per-element timeouts and need kmod-sched-core + kmod-cls-*; they bypass nftables like TC-BPF.
findings.technical_details: Verdict ordering by risk: nft set (in-tree, atomic) < flowtable < sockmap < TC-BPF < XDP < out-of-tree kmod. Fallbacks for kernels lacking support: sockmap -> Go splice (stdlib) -> io.Copy w/ pooled buffer; TC/XDP -> nft set; flowtable -> plain forward.

findings.description: cgroup/connect hooks (BPF_CGROUP_INET4_CONNECT / INET6_CONNECT) rewrite destinations of locally originated connects per-cgroup: useful to redirect an app's connections transparently on a host, but this project is a router where traffic is forwarded and not generated by local processes, so connect hooks are irrelevant to forwarded LAN traffic; they could replace the 'mihomo's own packets must not loop' fwmark/uid exemption but that already works.
findings.technical_details: Needs CGROUPS + CGROUP_BPF + mounted cgroup2, absent in generic OpenWrt config. Not worth it.

findings.topic: Other considerations: RAM, kmods and size on small devices
findings.description: eBPF adds kernel memory (JIT image pages, map memory charged to memlock/kernel; small) and, for TC/XDP, kmods. A sockmap psock allocates struct sk_psock (~ few hundred bytes) plus queues per socket plus a work item; with 1000s of long flows this is KBs not MBs. On 64-128 MB devices not a problem. On 16-32 MB devices (the Ultra profile) everything beyond sockmap is too costly (kmods), and the cilium/ebpf import cost (~1-2 MB) matters relative to a 16 MB binary target.
findings.technical_details: The hand-rolled raw-syscall loader (see F014) is the right path for an optional sockmap module if ever done; otherwise a separate helper binary (e.g. loaded by procd) keeps the core small and crash-isolated.

findings.topic: XDP generic and driver notes for the target SoCs
findings.description: Targets: mediatek filogic/mt7622/mt7623/mt7629 use mtk_eth_soc (XDP native only with page_pool), ramips mt7621 also uses mtk_eth_soc and has PAGE_POOL set in its config, so native XDP is plausible (unverified at runtime); ath79/qca955x etc. (ag71xx), qualcommax (ipq807x: edma / dp_soc, ppe offload via NSS), rockchip (stmmac/r8169/dwmac: stmmac supports XDP natively), ipq40xx (ipqess no XDP). Generic XDP works anywhere but is slower than native and does not skip skb allocation.
findings.technical_details: Only the mediatek and rockchip families plausibly support native XDP; qualcommax prefers its own HW offload (nss/ppe). Honest conclusion: XDP is not generally available on OpenWrt routers; do not depend on it.

findings.topic: Go integration cost: netpoller and fds
findings.description: Passing the raw fd to the BPF syscall requires syscall.RawConn.Control to get the socket fd without breaking the netpoller; after the sockets enter the sockmap, Go's netpoll would still be registered on those fds (epoll), and sockmap redirect intercepts data at tcp_read_skb in sk_data_ready, so epoll readability signals for the socket stop firing for payload but still fire for EOF? (unverified). Meaning net.Conn.Read must not be used afterwards, and the goroutine should only be waiting on Close/timeouts. A per-flow supervisor can use a pidfd-less approach: poll tcp_info state via getsockopt(TCP_INFO) on a timer for CLOSE_WAIT/ESTABLISHED, which costs a syscall per flow per tick.
findings.technical_details: This is the key engineering uncertainty for sockmap; requires an on-device prototype to resolve (see open questions).

findings.description: Per use: XDP: not worth it (bypasses firewall, driver-limited, no benefit over flowtable/PPE); TC-BPF classified-flow bypass: not worth it vs nft set + flowtable (needs kmods, bypasses fw4); sk_lookup as TPROXY replacement: not worth it (does not capture forwarded traffic); cgroup/connect: not worth it (router); sockmap splice of DIRECT proxied connections: optional module, only after an on-device benchmark shows gain over Go splice; Go splice already used by stdlib: baseline, ensure the relay passes bare *net.TCPConn.
findings.technical_details: Fallback chain: sockmap -> splice (io.Copy with TCPConn pairs) -> buffered copy. Gate sockmap by capability probing (BPF_MAP_CREATE SockHash + BPF_PROG_LOAD SkSKB) at startup and by kernel>=5.13 (stream_verdict) and self-test.

findings.description: Official docs consulted/relevant: docs.kernel.org/bpf/map_sockmap.html (sockmap/sockhash semantics), docs.kernel.org/bpf/prog_sk_lookup.html, docs.kernel.org/networking/nf_flowtable.html, docs.kernel.org/bpf/btf.html, ebpf.io/applications. I could not fetch these live in this session; claims referencing them are from the local kernel source and prior knowledge and are marked accordingly.

nft 'flow offload' is valid only in the FORWARD hook, only for TCP/UDP (GRE without NAT/key too), and only for confirmed conntrack entries. TCP requires nf_conntrack_tcp_established() and the current packet must not carry FIN or RST. Flows with a conntrack helper, IPS_SEQ_ADJUST or IPS_NAT_CLASH are refused.
findings.technical_details: nft_flow_offload_eval(): tcph->fin || tcph->rst || !nf_conntrack_tcp_established(ct) -> skip (nft_flow_offload.c:333-338); protonum switch allows only TCP, UDP, GRE (329-352); helper/SEQ_ADJUST/NAT_CLASH -> skip (355-357); !nf_ct_is_confirmed -> skip (360); IPS_OFFLOAD_BIT test_and_set (363). Hook validation: hook_mask = 1<<NF_INET_FORWARD (399-406). UDP has no established check (any confirmed UDP ct qualifies, in practice offloaded after the first reply makes it ASSURED only if the user rule requires 'ct state established'). Consequence: traffic delivered locally (INPUT) or originated locally (OUTPUT), which is every mihomo TPROXY/redirect/TUN connection, can never be offloaded.

findings.topic: Flowtable lifecycle, timeouts, FIN/RST, conntrack deletion
findings.description: A flow entry is torn down on: FIN/RST seen on the fast path, timeout expiry, or conntrack dying. When the ct is deleted (conntrack -D) the software fast path stops at once because flow_offload_lookup() returns NULL for a dying ct; the entry itself is reaped by the 1 s gc worker; for hardware offload it is first marked HW_DYING and removed from the device, then freed once HW_DEAD is set.
findings.technical_details: FIN/RST on the fast path: nf_flow_table_ip.c:31-34 -> flow_offload_teardown() (clears IPS_OFFLOAD, sets NF_FLOW_TEARDOWN, flow_offload_fixup_ct() restores ct timeout so the slow path takes over cleanly). flow_offload_lookup(): TEARDOWN flag -> NULL; nf_ct_is_dying(flow->ct) -> NULL (nf_flow_table_core.c:374-378) so a packet of a killed flow falls back to the normal stack (where, with ct gone, it is a NEW connection hitting prerouting rules again, i.e. TPROXY/redirect would now apply or a RST path). gc: nf_flow_offload_gc_step tears down if expired, ct dying or custom gc (core.c:425-431); gc interval HZ (core.c:458). Idle timeout NF_FLOW_TIMEOUT = 30 s (include/net/netfilter/nf_flow_table.h:189), refreshed on each packet; offload_timeout sysctl tunes ct timeouts while offloaded (core.c:174-199, 263-279). Hardware entries: NF_FLOW_HW_DYING set at nf_flow_table_offload.c:1129, HW_DEAD at 1062. So 'conntrack -D' (or nf_ct_iterate_cleanup via netlink delete) is an immediate invalidation in software and about 1 s in hardware (hypothesis for exact HW latency: depends on driver stats/flow_block callbacks, unmeasured).
findings.opus_note: linux:net/netfilter/nf_flow_table_core.c flow_offload_lookup returns NULL when nf_ct_is_dying

findings.topic: Flowtable hooks at ingress: offloaded flows skip prerouting, firewall and TPROXY
findings.description: The fw4 flowtable is declared 'hook ingress priority 0' on the listed devices; the software fast path forwards the packet from there, before inet prerouting/forward chains. Established offloaded flows therefore never see mangle/TPROXY/redirect rules, nor forward-chain rules, nor mihomo's marking. This is why a flow that was classified as PROXY must never be offloaded, and why invalidation must destroy the flow, not just edit rules.
findings.technical_details: firewall4 ruleset.uc:20-30 (flowtable ft { hook ingress priority 0; devices=...; flags offload if flow_offloading_hw }), and line 141: 'meta l4proto { tcp, udp } flow offload @ft;' as the FIRST rule of chain forward (before 'ct state established accept'). Only packets that already survived prerouting and reached the forward hook, in ESTABLISHED state, get added. A packet that was TPROXY'd or REDIRECT'd to a local socket never reaches FORWARD, so it is naturally never added. Danger case: a flow that began as plain-routed (bypass hit) and later should be PROXY (rule change) keeps being fast-pathed until torn down.

findings.topic: Path matrix: which paths can be offloaded
findings.description: Plain routed: yes (SW flowtable on all, HW only where a driver implements flow_block). TPROXY / REDIRECT to mihomo: no (local delivery, FORWARD hook never reached). TUN: no (routed into tun device, read in userspace; the reverse path is OUTPUT/local; also device not in the flowtable device list). DIRECT via mihomo: no (mihomo's outbound is a locally originated socket, OUTPUT hook, conntrack entry for the second leg is a local-out flow). PROXY via mihomo: no, and must not be. Only traffic that the kernel routes without ever delivering it to a local socket is offloadable.
findings.technical_details: Condition is structural: flow offload expression is validated only for the forward hook (nft_flow_offload.c:399-406). In a mihomo DIRECT connection there are two conntrack entries: client<->router:port (rewritten by redirect/TPROXY, local delivery) and router<->server (local OUT). Neither is a forwarded flow.

findings.topic: Why an already-terminated mihomo connection cannot be handed back
findings.description: After mihomo accepts, it holds two unrelated TCP connections (client-to-router with router ISN/window/options/timestamps, router-to-server with different ISN, MSS, window scaling, SACK, ECN, timestamps) plus buffered bytes in socket queues and possibly TLS sniffing state. The forward path would need seq/ack/option translation per direction (the kernel's flowtable does NAT only at L3/L4 port/addr level, no sequence rewriting; flows with IPS_SEQ_ADJUST are explicitly refused). Handing back would also require retiring both sockets silently (no FIN/RST, else peer notified) and recreating a conntrack entry in ESTABLISHED state without having seen the handshake: in-kernel there is no supported path for that (conntrack TCP_REPAIR-like injection exists only for socket state, not for the forwarding conntrack of the gateway).
findings.technical_details: Possible only with a splice-to-kernel scheme that does not exist: even TCP_REPAIR (restoring socket state) moves sockets between processes, not into the forwarding path. Equivalent trick (transparent re-injection with seq translation) is a custom eBPF/XDP program with per-flow offset maps; it still cannot be offloaded by flowtable and still runs per packet in the CPU, so it is a different, much larger project. UDP is slightly different: a DIRECT UDP association has no sequence state, but the same two-conntrack-entry structure and NAT mismatch (source port rewritten by mihomo's socket) apply, and QUIC connection migration/ID semantics are preserved only if the real client address stays on the wire. Conclusion: classification-after-the-fact cannot hand off the current connection; only FUTURE connections can be diverted.
findings.opus_note: consistent with F001: local delivery (TPROXY/REDIRECT) is never in FORWARD

findings.topic: Realistic mechanism: pre-interception exact-tuple bypass set
findings.description: Mihomo classifies connection N, then installs a set element that the PREROUTING interception rule tests first (return/accept before TPROXY/redirect). Connection N itself continues through userspace; connections N+1.. to the same key are plain routed, then SW/HW flowtable-offloaded. Keys: choose granularity by policy certainty. Concatenation daddr . dport (+ proto) is the minimum; saddr . daddr . dport is safer (per-device policy); full 4-tuple is meaningless for a not-yet-existing connection (ephemeral sport).
findings.technical_details: nft set 'type ipv4_addr . ipv4_addr . inet_service; flags timeout; timeout 5m' (+ a v6 twin) with a rule 'ip saddr . ip daddr . tcp dport @direct_fast return' placed before the interception rule in a priority mangle (-150) prerouting chain; the same rule with 'meta l4proto' split for udp. Dynamic (kernel-side) insertion is also possible with 'update @s { ... timeout 5m }' but only for data-plane triggers, not for userspace verdicts, so userspace must add. clashwrt already runs this exact structure: 'ip daddr @bypass4 return' (fw.sh:477-478) with a static interval set (fw.sh:538) and a timeout set bypass4_dns (flags timeout; timeout 1d, fw.sh:539), refilled via nft -f batches by setctl.sh (flush set + add element, setctl.sh:797-799).

findings.topic: Go APIs: metacubex/nftables and google/nftables set updates
findings.description: The fork's indirect dependency github.com/metacubex/nftables@v0.0.0-20260426003805-208c2c1ba2cb (a google/nftables derivative; module path used by sing-tun@v0.4.28 redirect_nftables_*.go) supports everything needed: sets with HasTimeout/Timeout/Dynamic/Concatenation/Interval, SetAddElements, SetDeleteElements, FlushSet, GetSetElements, and flowtables (flowtable.go). Elements carry a per-element Timeout and Expires. Updates are sent over a netlink batch; the Conn buffers messages until Flush().
findings.technical_details: set.go: type SetElement{Key, Val, KeyEnd, IntervalEnd, Timeout, Expires, Counter...} (277-296); (cc *Conn) SetAddElements (376), AddSet (496, flags incl. Concatenation 537, Timeout 559-561), SetDeleteElements (704), FlushSet (727), GetSetElements (972). Per-element timeout is written only when the set has HasTimeout (422-424). Concatenated keys must be hand-packed as padded 4-byte-aligned fields (v4 addr 4B, port 2B padded to 4B on the wire: hypothesis, check against nft's own encoding before use) since the library does not build the concat key for you. Note: the module is currently an indirect dep, so enabling this in the fork adds sing-tun's already-linked package to the build; a direct dep would be only a go.mod change. Cost per update: one netlink sendmsg per Flush (batch many adds per Flush); about tens of microseconds of syscall plus kernel set insertion (hash set, O(1)); not benchmarked here.

findings.topic: Mihomo's existing route-exclude-address-set and why it is not enough
findings.description: Mihomo/sing-tun already has RouteExcludeAddressSet (tun config) which feeds an nft set checked by sing-tun's auto-redirect rules, but it is a STATIC address-set mechanism (CIDR lists) and only exists when mihomo owns the firewall (auto-route + auto-redirect). It does not provide per-connection verdict-driven insertion or invalidation.
findings.technical_details: fork config/config.go:298 (RouteExcludeAddressSet) and :1719. clashwrt's own comment in setctl.sh header states route-exclude-address-set requires auto-route and auto-redirect and is incompatible with routing-mark, hence clashwrt keeps its own set. A dynamic exact-tuple bypass module would be a separate component in the core (e.g. a `fastpath` package) wired to the rule matcher result.

findings.description: A domain-based DIRECT verdict must not become an IP-level exemption unless that exact IP is provably only reachable under that verdict. On a shared CDN IP, domain A (DIRECT) and domain B (PROXY) hit the same address; bypassing by daddr would send B's traffic direct (leak and policy violation). The bypass key therefore needs either (a) per-connection proof that the whole IP . port is policy-uniform, or (b) a poison rule that blocks insertion.
findings.technical_details: Safe insertion criteria (proposal): insert only when (1) the verdict came from a rule whose result is independent of the domain (GEOIP/IP-CIDR/DST-PORT/PROCESS-NAME-by-source-IP) OR (2) the DNS answer cache maps this IP to only domains with the same verdict (mihomo already keeps ip->domain mapping for fake-ip and for sniffing), AND no rule in the config could yield a different outcome for any domain (a global check at config load: if any DOMAIN/ RULE-SET-domain rule routes to a non-DIRECT outcome, mark domain-derived inserts 'tainted' and only allow IP-derived verdicts). Reverse hazard: a DNS answer that later returns a PROXY domain on an IP already in the set must delete the element (mihomo sees every resolution through its DNS server; hook there). With ECH/HTTP3 the SNI is invisible, so sniffer-based domain verdicts cannot support (b).

findings.description: In fake-ip mode clients connect to fake addresses; the kernel cannot route those to the real server, and a bypass keyed on a fake IP would just black-hole. A DIRECT fast path needs the client to hold the real IP, so the DNS server must hand out real-IP answers for domains whose verdict is DIRECT (fake-ip-filter semantics, reverse of the usual direction), accepting that the domain->verdict mapping must be known at DNS time (rule-based on domain; GEOIP-derived DIRECT is unknown at DNS time).
findings.technical_details: Design consequence: only domain-decidable DIRECT (DOMAIN/ DOMAIN-SUFFIX/ RULE-SET domain) can be real-ip answered. IP-based DIRECT (GEOIP,RU) needs resolution first; with real-ip mode the client already has the real IP and the kernel-level set can cover it by CIDR (static, like clashwrt's bypass4 interval set). Also, DNS leak: real-ip answers for DIRECT domains must come from a DNS upstream consistent with policy (direct nameservers), and PROXY domains stay fake-ip so no real-IP leaks occur. Hypothesis: mixed mode adds complexity and is the fragile part, so a profile may restrict the fast path to real-IP mode.

findings.description: IPv6: needs a parallel ipv6_addr set and the same ordering; the flowtable handles IPv6 forward (nft_flow_offload.c:250-251) and MediaTek PPE supports IPv6 5-tuple (mtk_foe_entry_set_ipv6_tuple). Without NAT, IPv6 clients have globally routable source addresses, so a bypass key of saddr . daddr is natural. UDP/QUIC: a UDP flow is offload-eligible once confirmed; QUIC to a DIRECT destination is safe to bypass once the verdict is known, but a PROXY-policy QUIC flow must be dropped/blocked first (or the first Initial must be intercepted) since the bypass set is consulted per packet, not per connection: the first packet of a flow decides the conntrack path. Sniffer: the sniffer needs the first bytes through userspace to learn the SNI, so SNI-based decisions are possible only from connection N onward; the first connection per (src,dst,dport) always goes through mihomo.
findings.technical_details: nft_flow_offload.c:242-251 set fl.u.ip4/ip6 tuple per family. Race: between mihomo's decision on connection N and the set insertion, the kernel may route a retransmitted SYN or a second parallel connection (browsers open several) to mihomo, which is harmless (consistent verdict). The unsafe race is the reverse: PROXY verdict follows a DIRECT insertion on the same key (policy changed, DNS answer remapped). That is covered by F013 invalidation.

findings.topic: Set update vs first packet race
findings.description: Netlink set insertion becomes visible to the data plane at transaction commit (nf_tables uses a generation counter; a batch is atomic). A connection's first SYN either sees the old or the new set content, never a partial one. Exposure: insertion latency (Go goroutine + syscall + commit) means the first few connections still go through mihomo; this is a performance, not a safety, race. Safety race is the opposite direction (stale DIRECT element kept after policy flips).
findings.technical_details: Mitigation set: (a) short element timeout (for example 30-120 s, refreshed only on a new classification) bounds staleness even if mihomo dies; (b) element add runs in a batched, non-blocking worker so dial latency is unaffected; (c) config reload runs 'flush set; conntrack delete for bypassed tuples' before the new rule table goes live. The kernel set timeout is evaluated lazily on lookup: expired elements are not matched.

findings.topic: Invalidation on rule change and mihomo crash
findings.description: On config/rule/proxy-group change or when policy cannot be guaranteed: flush the bypass sets, then delete conntrack entries that were offloaded through the bypass (a flushed set only stops NEW flows; established offloaded flows keep forwarding past all rules). Deletion via NFNL_SUBSYS_CTNETLINK delete (conntrack -D with a source/dest filter) makes the ct dying and flow_offload_lookup stop matching immediately (software). Mihomo crash: bypass entries remain in the kernel; with kernel-side timeouts the DIRECT shortcut persists until expiry, and offloaded established flows continue to work. This is a fail-open for destinations that were classified DIRECT only, which is acceptable when classifications were DIRECT; the dangerous part is the INTERCEPTION rules (TPROXY/redirect) pointing at a dead listener, which is an existing clashwrt watchdog problem ('autobypass' flag, fw.sh:47-52), not new.
findings.technical_details: Because a flow-offload entry is created from a ct and the ct holds the policy state, the clean invalidation primitive is ct deletion (by tuple). Mark-based selective deletion: tag bypass-accepted packets with a ct mark (e.g. 'ct mark set 0x...' in the bypass rule) and delete all ct with that mark via ctnetlink (conntrack -D -m <mark>); this is O(conntrack table) once per rule change and avoids tracking per-flow tuples in Go. SW flowtable also honours NF_FLOW_TEARDOWN set when the ct is killed (core.c:429). Kill-switch semantics (hypothesis, design choice): on crash with strict mode, the supervisor must flush the bypass set AND the ct entries, otherwise 'kill switch' leaves a DIRECT shortcut open for up to the element timeout.

findings.description: MediaTek is the one family where upstream nf_flowtable 'flags offload' maps to hardware: the mtk_eth_soc driver implements ndo_setup_tc for flow blocks and mtk_ppe_offload.c programs FOE entries (IPv4 and IPv6 tuples, NAT, VLAN/PPPoE, DSA tags). Enabled in OpenWrt for mediatek targets (NET_MEDIATEK_SOC with WED def_bool). WED (Wireless Ethernet Dispatch) is a separate hardware path for MT7915/MT7916/MT7615 Wi-Fi which lets PPE-forwarded flows skip the CPU to wireless; it requires CONFIG_NET_MEDIATEK_SOC_WED and PPE.
findings.technical_details: mtk_eth_soc.c:4643 .ndo_setup_tc = mtk_eth_setup_tc; mtk_ppe_offload.c:267 mtk_flow_offload_replace (parses flow_rule: meta, control, basic, ipv4/ipv6 addrs, ports); mtk_ppe_offload.c:101-295 handles WED only if IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_NET_MEDIATEK_SOC_WED). OpenWrt: generic/config-6.12:4390 '# CONFIG_NF_FLOW_TABLE is not set' (generic default), enabled via kmod-nf-flow (netfilter.mk:199-210 CONFIG_NF_FLOW_TABLE and NF_FLOW_TABLE_HW); mediatek filogic/mt7622/mt7629/mt7623 config set NET_MEDIATEK_SOC=y (mt7621 and other ramips use ramips ethernet and are SOFTWARE-only: hypothesis, check target config). SoC coverage: which have a working PPE: MT7622 (PPE v1), MT7623 (hypothesis), MT7981/MT7986/MT7988 (NETSYS v2/v3, the filogic target). Rate: wire speed forwarding, on filogic 2.5G/10G ports. HW NAT PPE has a flow-table size limit (order of 16k entries per PPE; unverified), hardware flows beyond the table fall back to software flowtable.

findings.description: ipq40xx (IPQ4018/4019) has no hardware NAT in OpenWrt; software flowtable only. ipq807x/ipq60xx (qualcommax) have NSS/PPE offload only through vendor out-of-tree stacks (qca-nss-drv/ECM from the NSS-OpenWrt forks, e.g. the 'NSS builds'), not the standard nf_flowtable hw offload, and these stacks are not in OpenWrt mainline. ECM takes over conntrack-based flow acceleration with its own sysctls and does not honour nft sets in the same way.
findings.technical_details: In openwrt v25.12.6 sparse: no NSS packages in target/linux/qualcommax tree (grep for NSS/OFFLOAD in qualcommax/ipq40xx configs returned nothing relevant). Recommendation for a fast path: treat Qualcomm as software-flowtable only unless the user installs an NSS build, and detect it (presence of /sys/kernel/debug/ecm or kmod qca-nss-ecm) to DISABLE the bypass design since ECM can accelerate flows created before the bypass set was edited and has its own invalidation (hypothesis).

findings.description: Realtek rtl838x/rtl93xx: the switch ASIC can route L3 but OpenWrt's DSA driver (rtl838x) exposes switching only for the router CPU path; L3 hardware offload is not exposed to nf_flowtable (hypothesis, not confirmed in sparse tree). Broadcom: proprietary CTF/Runner/Flow Cache (in vendor SDK firmware), not in OpenWrt; a Broadcom router running OpenWrt uses the kernel only (software). Rockchip (RK3328/RK3399/RK3568/RK3588): software flowtable only; high CPU throughput makes it adequate. ramips mt7621 (the most common cheap OpenWrt SoC) has no PPE in mainline: software flowtable only. ath79: software.
findings.technical_details: Standard flowtable HW offload requires an ndo_setup_tc/TC_SETUP_FT or flow_block callback in the NIC/switch driver; the sparse tree has this only for mediatek. Vendor stacks (Qualcomm ECM/NSS, Broadcom FlowCache/CTF, Realtek SDK L3) are independent from nf_flowtable and each needs its own invalidation, which a fast-path safety design cannot assume.

findings.description: SW flowtable keeps traffic on the CPU, so an egress cake qdisc on the WAN device still shapes fast-pathed packets, and ingress shaping through ifb/tc mirred runs at tc-ingress which is before netfilter ingress in the receive path (so flowtable does not hide packets from it: hypothesis from netdev receive ordering, verify on device). HW offload (PPE) forwards without the CPU; qdiscs and tc filters on those flows are bypassed, so cake no longer shapes them (OpenWrt guidance: SQM and hardware flow offloading conflict). clashwrt already notes that a DIRECT rule in mihomo collapses all hosts behind one address (the router) so cake cannot tell hosts apart, a reason the bypass design is attractive even in software mode.
findings.technical_details: clashwrt setctl.sh header: 'a DIRECT rule inside mihomo is not a fast path... collapses every device behind one address, so a shaper like cake can no longer tell hosts apart. Traffic excluded here never reaches mihomo at all.' Per-host fairness for DIRECT traffic is regained for both SW flowtable and plain routing. With HW flow offload and SQM enabled, the safe default is software flowtable and warn when 'flags offload' is on with an active sqm instance.

findings.topic: DNS leak and policy consistency of the bypass
findings.description: A bypass entry stops the kernel from sending packets to mihomo, but DNS resolution itself continues to go through mihomo's DNS server (or dnsmasq). The leak risks are: (1) DNS queries of bypassed clients still reach upstreams via the proxy or direct per DNS policy, so policy for DNS must be explicit and not be shortcut by the bypass set (port 53/853/443-DoH must never be in the key space); (2) a bypassed destination discovered through a proxied DNS answer (PROXY resolver, geo-DNS) may be a different IP than the DIRECT resolver returns, so cache-poisoned or geo-mismatched CDN addresses can be bypassed: key insertion should require that the answer came from the policy-matching resolver (hypothesis).
findings.technical_details: Implementation constraint: exclude dport 53/853 and DoH IPs from insertion (clashwrt already keeps doh4 reject set, fw.sh:459). Insert on dial success of a DIRECT outbound, not on rule match alone, so unreachable addresses are never promoted.

findings.topic: Cost model: what the fast path saves
findings.description: A DIRECT connection through mihomo costs two sockets, user-space copy (splice is not used by mihomo's relay; it uses copy buffers), and conntrack twice. Offloaded flows cost one conntrack entry and a hash lookup in the flowtable per packet. No measured numbers collected here; claims of throughput gain are unverified.
findings.technical_details: No benchmark was run (no root, no NIC). Needed experiment: iperf3 through a DIRECT rule in mihomo vs plain routing vs SW flowtable on the target SoC (mt7621, mt7981, ipq40xx, rk3568). Treat as hypothesis until measured.

findings.topic: Insertion point and flowtable device list
findings.description: A bypass hit makes the packet fall out of the clashwrt mangle chain and into the normal path; to be offloaded it must reach the fw4 forward chain 'flow offload @ft' rule and the devices must be in the flowtable device list. The bypass set must therefore live in a chain that runs BEFORE interception (prerouting mangle/ raw) and must not terminate with 'accept' in a way that skips fw4's forward evaluation (a 'return' in the clashwrt chain is correct; a verdict in the prerouting base chain does not affect the later forward base chain).
findings.technical_details: fw4 chain forward flow offload rule at ruleset.uc:141 runs at 'hook forward priority filter'; clashwrt's own table is separate ('inet clashwrt', fw.sh:477), so fw4 offload and the clashwrt bypass cooperate by construction. Check: fw4 only adds flow offload when flow_offloading is enabled in /etc/config/firewall defaults (fw4.resolve_offload_devices, ruleset.uc:2).

findings.topic: Container-aware GOMAXPROCS is off for this module
findings.description: Go 1.25 added cgroup-CPU-limit-aware default GOMAXPROCS and periodic updates (containermaxprocs, updatemaxprocs). Both are GODEBUG settings whose defaults depend on the main module's go.mod 'go' line; the fork has 'go 1.20' and no godebug block, so both are 0 (old behaviour).
findings.technical_details: internal/godebugs/table.go lists containermaxprocs/updatemaxprocs/decoratemappings with Changed:25, Old:"0"; with go.mod go<1.25 Old applies. godebug.md documents the semantics. runtime/cgroup_linux.go reads /proc/self/cgroup + mountinfo once and polls the limit file. On a plain OpenWrt router (no cpu cgroup quota) the new feature changes nothing anyway: GOMAXPROCS = CPU count/affinity. mihomo main.go:99 uses uber automaxprocs v1.6.0 (go.mod:62) that does the cgroup quota rounding itself (also a no-op on bare routers; it pulls code and a cgroup parse at startup). Also decoratemappings=0 under go 1.20 (no [anon: Go:] names in /proc/maps).

findings.description: Green Tea GC was an opt-in experiment in Go 1.25 (GOEXPERIMENT=greenteagc), became the default in Go 1.26 (from release notes, not re-verified locally), and in the local Go 1.27.3 tree it is in the baseline experiment set (still switchable at build time with GOEXPERIMENT=nogreenteagc). Also baseline in 1.27: SizeSpecializedMalloc, RandomizedHeapBase64, JSONv2.
findings.technical_details: internal/buildcfg/exp.go:80-88 baseline {GreenTeaGC:true, JSONv2:true, SizeSpecializedMalloc:true, RandomizedHeapBase64:true}. Green Tea scans spans (8 KiB) rather than individual objects, improving memory locality; the advertised gain is 10-40% less GC CPU on GC-heavy programs, with the main benefit for many-core machines and small-object heaps; effect on a 10-30 MB heap on 1-2 cores is expected to be small. Upstream CI builds mihomo with Go 1.26 (build.yml:167,181) so it already gets Green Tea. JSONv2 baseline means encoding/json v1 is implemented on top of json/v2 in 1.27: possible binary size/init change (unmeasured). Experiment: my hello server with GOEXPERIMENT=nogreenteagc gave identical RSS (30584 vs 30616 kB), i.e. no visible RSS effect at this scale.
findings.opus_note: Green Tea GC is ON by default in Go 1.27 (go:internal/buildcfg/exp.go:86 GreenTeaGC: true in baseline). 1.26 status not re-checked.

findings.topic: GC pacing: GOGC, heap minimum, GOMEMLIMIT semantics
findings.description: Default GOGC=100 with a 4 MiB minimum heap goal: a small program GCs when live heap doubles but never below 4 MiB total heap. An opt-in experiment HeapMinimum512KiB (Go 1.27 tree) lowers this to 512 KiB; it is NOT in the baseline. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft limit on total Go-runtime-mapped memory (heap+stacks+runtime structures, not binary text, not kernel buffers); as the limit nears, GC frequency rises and the scavenger returns memory; a GC CPU limiter (50% cap, leaky bucket) prevents a death spiral where the program thrashes in GC, after which the limit is exceeded rather than the program stalling.
findings.technical_details: runtime/mgcpacer.go:58-60 defaultHeapMinimum = 4<<20 unless GOEXPERIMENT=heapminimum512kib (internal/goexperiment/flags.go:79-84). runtime/mgclimit.go:13-16 'very conservative limit of 50%'. runtime/mgcscavenge.go:54-62 background scavenger targets (100-reduceExtraPercent)/100*memoryLimit when a limit is set. Consequence for routers: GOMEMLIMIT must be set well above the live set or GC runs continuously until the limiter cuts it off; set it relative to expected peak (live heap + stacks + ~25% slack), not to total RAM. Process-kill (OOM) is not prevented; the limit is a throttle. Experiment: hello net server at GOMAXPROCS=1, 500 conns, GOGC=50 and GOMEMLIMIT=16MiB gave 30620/30356 kB RSS vs 30616 kB default - dominated by my own 32 KiB client buffers, so inconclusive for GOGC.

findings.topic: Scavenger and returning memory to the OS
findings.description: Linux default release advice is MADV_DONTNEED (debug.madvdontneed=1 default since 1.16), so RSS falls when the scavenger releases pages, unlike MADV_FREE. The background scavenger paces itself to ~1% of mutator CPU and releases down to roughly retain = (1+retainExtraPercent)*heapGoal-ish, so RSS lags heap by minutes after a spike; debug.FreeOSMemory() forces a GC plus full scavenge. mihomo only exposes FreeOSMemory on the debug-mode API route /debug/gc.
findings.technical_details: runtime/runtime1.go:407 'default to MADV_DONTNEED' sets debug.madvdontneed=1; runtime/mem_linux.go:38-64 sysUnusedOS chooses MADV_FREE (if madvdontneed==0) else MADV_DONTNEED. runtime/mgcscavenge.go:15 scavengePercent soft cap of mutator time; :74-79 releases in huge-page-aware chunks. fork:hub/route/server.go:109-113 PUT /debug/gc calls debug.FreeOSMemory() only when log level is debug. A periodic low-priority FreeOSMemory (e.g. after connections drop below a threshold, or every N minutes while idle) is an easy RSS reduction on routers; cost = one full GC + page-faults on regrowth. Combining GOMEMLIMIT also makes the background scavenger more aggressive.

findings.topic: Experiment: hello net server RSS vs GOMAXPROCS
findings.description: Static amd64 hello server (2.3 MB binary): idle RSS 4.7 MB at GOMAXPROCS=1, 6.8 MB at 2 (noisy), 4.8 MB at 4; threads 3/4/6. So P count barely matters for RSS (per-P mcache is small); the cost of more Ps is threads and scheduler spinning, not memory. With 500 loopback connections (1000 sockets, 500 goroutines with 32 KiB client buffers) RSS was 30.6 MB for every P count.
findings.technical_details: Built CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -buildvcs=false -ldflags '-s -w', Go 1.27.3, /proc/self/status after a forced GC. The 500-conn run is polluted by my 500x32 KiB client buffers (16 MB) so the net per-connection-pair cost (2 goroutines + conn structs + netpoll) is about (30.6-4.7-16)/500 ~ 20 KB -- upper bound, rough, hypothesis. Single run each, no repetition. Files: scratchpad/go_runtime_memory/hello/main.go.

findings.topic: Experiment: idle RSS of the full fork (amd64) and init() cost
findings.description: Fork built with -tags with_gvisor, started with an empty config dir (no network wait), had VmRSS ~46 MB and 14 threads about 1.5 s after start. GODEBUG=inittrace=1 shows 453 package inits allocating 1.76 MB of heap in total; the top: metacubex/gopacket/layers 466 KB (+ 2.6 MB .bss tables EthernetTypeMetadata/PPPTypeMetadata), google/pprof/profile 154 KB, easytier api/instance 82 KB, mieru appctlpb 56 KB, goupnp/soap 55 KB, gobwas/ws 54 KB, easytier peer_rpc 53 KB, tailscale varz 34 KB, regexp2/syntax 29 KB.
findings.technical_details: Method: GODEBUG=inittrace=1 ./mihomo -v (init lines on stderr: 'init pkg @t ms, X ms clock, N bytes, M allocs'). Individual init costs are small (<0.4 ms), so init heap is ~4% of 46 MB; the bulk of RSS is touched binary pages, runtime/GC structures, and later config/rule/geodata load. crypto/internal/fips140/drbg.memory is a 32 MiB .noptrbss symbol (nm: 33554432 B) - bss is virtual and not resident unless touched, but inflates VSZ. NOTE: measured with an empty config; real RSS depends on geosite/mmdb/rule-sets. Not a router measurement.
findings.opus_note: independent run: official amd64 idle RSS 44.7 MB (mem.sh) vs agent 46 MB

findings.topic: Fixed runtime overhead: stacks, mcache, GC workers
findings.description: Goroutine minimum stack is 2 KiB (grows by copying, doubling; shrunk by GC if under 1/4 used). Each P has an mcache (small, in non-GC memory). Background GC worker goroutines (one per P, dedicated or fractional/idle) and sysmon/scavenger/bgsweep goroutines exist regardless of load. Idle process: ~3 threads at GOMAXPROCS=1 in my hello test.
findings.technical_details: runtime/stack.go:78 stackMin = 2048; runtime/mcache.go:20 type mcache (per-P, allocated by procresize). Real TLS/proxy relay goroutines usually grow to 8-16 KiB stacks (crypto, bufio.Copy frames). Per relayed TCP connection mihomo.Relay starts 1 extra goroutine (the calling one is the second) (fork:common/net/sing.go:69-92), plus listener/proxy goroutines for the outbound (e.g. TLS read loop, mux), 2 net.Conn structs, netpoll entries, pooled buffers only while a Read is blocked. Estimated 20-40 KB heap per proxied connection (hypothesis, unmeasured with real mihomo).

findings.description: The tag (which the fork exposes in feature tags) changes only: (1) pool.RelayBufferSize 32K->16K and pool.UDPBufferSize 16K->8K (fork common/pool/buffer_low_memory.go vs buffer_standard.go); (2) sing buf.BufferSize 32K->16K and buf.UDPBufferSize 16K->8K; (3) sing common.LowMemory=true makes bufio.Copy / CopyExtended / CopyOnce always take the copyWaitWithPool path (wait for readability, then take a buffer) instead of preallocating. Nothing in sing-tun, sing-mux, gvisor or quic-go references the tag (grep found none).
findings.technical_details: sing@v0.5.8 common/low_memory.go, common/buf/buffer_low_memory.go; bufio/copy.go:110 and :269 and copy_once.go:16 use '!needCopy || common.LowMemory'; fork constant/features/low_memory.go + tags.go:7. Users of the fork constants: UDP read paths (common/net/packet/packet.go:67, listener/tproxy/*, listener/tunnel/udp.go:62, component/resolver/relay.go:30, adapter/outbound/masque.go:379, transport/snell, trojan.go:195) and RelayBufferSize in simple-obfs/ssr/vmess chunk/aead. Tradeoff: smaller buffers = more syscalls per MB (higher CPU, lower peak), not applicable to large TUN MTU 9000 packets > 8 KiB UDP buffer (possible truncation risk of UDP > 8 KiB; unverified). sizes of arm64 binaries with/without the tag are identical (56492156 bytes).

findings.description: common/pool is a power-of-two sync.Pool allocator (64 B..64 KiB, 11 classes, pointer-to-array so no allocation on Put) installed as sing's buf.DefaultAllocator; >64 KiB falls back to make(). sync.Pool is cleared across two GC cycles, so a burst of connections returns buffers to the GC and RSS depends on GC cadence (another reason to keep GOGC moderate). Hot paths with per-op make(): transport/socks5/socks5.go (lines 111,132,137,214,319,388-400,439-445: handshake/address buffers, per UDP packet at 388-445), pool.GetBuffer returns bytes.Buffer pooled objects.
findings.technical_details: fork:common/pool/alloc.go:20-60; alloc.go Get returns nil for size 0; sing.go:3-6 init sets buf.DefaultAllocator. The relay path itself is allocation-light in non-LowMemory mode only when the source implements ReadWaiter; otherwise CopyExtendedWithPool allocates a 32 KiB buffer per read cycle and each blocked Read holds one (sing bufio/copy.go:159-190), so N idle non-ReadWaiter (e.g. TLS-wrapped) conns hold N x 32 KiB: an important RSS driver at 1000+ connections; with_low_memory halves this and uses wait-then-read where available. A cheaper fix is a first-read small buffer (e.g. 2-4 KiB, grow on full read) for idle connections (opportunity, hypothesis).

findings.topic: Binary size today: far above 16 MB
findings.description: Stripped (-s -w -buildid=) fork with only with_gvisor: amd64 61 MB, arm64 56.5 MB, arm GOARM=7 56.0 MB, mipsle softfloat 62.8 MB, riscv64 53.1 MB. arm64 -buildmode=pie: 63.4 MB (+12%). Section split (amd64): .text 25.2 MB, .gopclntab 20.1 MB, .noptrdata 7.6 MB (6.85 MB is easytier artifact blob), .rodata 1.7 MB. By-package symbol sizes (amd64 nm): easytier artifact 6.85 MB data, gopacket/layers 6.8 MB (tables), text of tailscale 2.26 MB, wazero 1.08 MB, gvisor 0.81 MB, protobuf impl 0.37 MB.
findings.technical_details: Method: go build -tags with_gvisor -trimpath -ldflags '-s -w -buildid=' per GOARCH; readelf -S -W; go tool nm -size -sort size | grouped by import path. Fork contains tailscale, easytier, zerotier, mieru, wazero (wasm engine), reedsolomon, jls/restls etc. (go.mod). pclntab (function table + file/line tables) is ~1/3 of the file and is NOT removed by -s -w (only DWARF/symtab are). Reaching <=16 MB needs build-tag pruning of whole protocol families (~30-40 MB), and likely also removing geodata/embedded blobs. Absolute gc-compiled sizes here are for the whole feature set, not an optimized profile.
findings.opus_note: bench/size.sh reproduces the per-arch sizes byte-for-byte for official tags

findings.topic: Build flags and what each does
findings.description: -s strips symtab, -w strips DWARF, -buildid= makes builds reproducible (tiny size), -trimpath removes local paths (slightly smaller, reproducible; pclntab still stores file names). CGO_ENABLED=0 gives static, no libc (fork Makefile already does this). Default linux/arm64 and mips executables are non-PIE static; -buildmode=pie adds relocations/dynamic sections (measured +12% on arm64) and is not needed on OpenWrt routers for size/speed. GOAMD64 matters for x86 only. -checklinkname=0 only needed if a dependency uses go:linkname into restricted runtime symbols; I did not test it on this fork (unverified).
findings.technical_details: Fork Makefile:14-18 uses -tags with_gvisor -trimpath -ldflags '-w -s -buildid=' and CGO_ENABLED=0. Go linker has no LTO. Size levers beyond flags: build tags per feature (biggest), UPX-style compression (external; runtime decompress cost is RAM-expensive on routers because the whole binary is resident after decompress; hypothesis), moving rule/geo data out of the binary, -gcflags='-l' (disable inlining; may shrink a few %, costs CPU; untested). GOEXPERIMENT can drop features only rarely. No LTO exists for gc; gccgo/TinyGo are not viable: gccgo lags the language (no current-Go support and uncertain generics/runtime parity) and TinyGo lacks parts of reflect/net/crypto-tls/unsafe patterns heavily used by mihomo, sing, quic-go and gvisor (probable; not tested).

findings.topic: What dead-code elimination cannot remove here
findings.description: text/template and html/template are absent from the binary (0 symbols), so the method-reachability pessimization from them is not present; reflect.Value.Method is present (2 symbols) - any reflect Method/MethodByName with a non-constant name makes the linker keep all exported methods of reachable types, which blunts DCE for e.g. protobuf, yaml, JSON codecs. Interface method calls keep method sets of every type converted to an interface; package-level var initializers and init() with side effects (registries in tailscale, protobuf descriptors, gopacket layer tables) are always retained once a package is imported.
findings.technical_details: Measured with go tool nm on mihomo_sym: text/template 0, html/template 0, net/http/pprof 0 matches, reflect.Value.Method 2, tailscale 7345 symbols, protobuf 2220, gvisor 3677, wazero 2060, easytier 1504, mieru 1083. The proven way to cut size is not importing packages (build tags + stubs), since one import drags in package-level registrations. Find size per package: go tool nm -size -sort size | aggregate by import path, or go-size-analyzer (gsa) / go tool nm; use go build -ldflags=-dumpdep to see who pulls a package (I did not run gsa; not installed).

findings.topic: Crypto assembly per architecture in Go 1.27 stdlib
findings.description: crypto/internal/fips140 AES, AES-GCM (GHASH), SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-3 have assembly on arm64 (and amd64, s390x, ppc64x for some; riscv64 has only SHA-256/512 + subtle xor; loong64 xor). There is NO assembly for 32-bit ARM (GOARM=5/6/7), mips, mipsle, mips64 in AES/GCM/SHA/xor/chacha8rand/nistec paths: they use pure-Go generic code (aes_noasm.go, gcm_noasm.go, sha256block_noasm.go).
findings.technical_details: go:crypto/internal/fips140/aes/aes_arm64.s, ctr_arm64.s, aes/gcm/gcm_arm64.s (build tag '(amd64||arm64)&&!purego', aes/gcm/gcm_asm.go:1); sha256/sha256block_arm64.s + sha256block_riscv64.s; sha512 same; sha3/sha3_arm64.s; subtle/xor_arm64.s,xor_riscv64.s; internal/chacha8rand has amd64/arm64/loong64/riscv64 only. nistec p256 asm: amd64, arm64, ppc64le, s390x (no arm/mips/riscv64) so TLS/QUIC ECDHE P-256 handshakes are slow in pure Go on MIPS/ARMv7. Consequence: AES-128/256-GCM (SS aes-gcm, VMess aes-128-gcm, Trojan/TLS 1.3 AES) on MIPS/ARMv7 runs generic table-less Go AES+GHASH; hardware-accelerated only on arm64 (when CPU has AES/PMULL extensions - not all cheap SoCs, e.g. some Cortex-A53 have crypto ext, others do not).

findings.topic: ChaCha20-Poly1305 assembly in the fork's dependencies
findings.description: x/crypto v0.33.0 (in the fork) has chacha20 NEON assembly for arm64 (also ppc64x, s390x) and poly1305 assembly only for amd64, ppc64x, s390x - so on arm64 ChaCha20 is vectorized but Poly1305 is pure Go; chacha20poly1305 combined AVX2 assembly is amd64-only. On ARMv7 and MIPS both are pure Go. The fork also imports github.com/metacubex/chacha (chacha.go only, pure Go; its poly1305 dir is separate); which code path each protocol uses (SS chacha20-ietf-poly1305 vs VLESS/VMess) was not traced.
findings.technical_details: x/crypto@v0.33.0: chacha20/chacha_arm64.s, chacha_ppc64x.s, chacha_s390x.s; internal/poly1305/sum_amd64.s, sum_ppc64x.s, sum_s390x.s; chacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305_amd64.s. Hence a MIPS/ARMv7 router will generally be faster with AES-128-GCM only if arm64 AES ext exist, otherwise ChaCha20 (designed for CPUs without AES instructions) is the better default on ARMv7/MIPS - but both are slow in Go without SIMD; 'none'/plain TLS-over-TCP-passthrough is far cheaper. Quantitative MB/s on target hardware: unmeasured.

findings.description: GOARM=5 uses software floating point and kernel helpers for some atomics; GOARM=6 adds VFP; GOARM=7 uses VFPv3 and native LDREX/STREX atomics. The fork Makefile builds v5/v6/v7. GOMIPS=softfloat is the safe choice for OpenWrt MIPS targets (OpenWrt mips_24kc/mipsel_24kc packages are soft-float ABI; a hardfloat binary on an FPU-less core dies with SIGILL, softfloat on an FPU core only costs float speed). mihomo is integer-heavy so softfloat is the proposed default (hypothesis). GORISCV64 picks rva20u64 (default) or rva22u64 baseline; GOMIPS64 has the same softfloat/hardfloat switch.
findings.technical_details: Fork Makefile:113-131 builds arm v5/v6/v7 and mips/mipsle softfloat+hardfloat. Binary size from my cross-build: arm7 56.0 MB, mipsle softfloat 62.8 MB (MIPS code is larger, no compressed instructions). Details of cmd/go env vars from go.dev/cmd/go and internal/buildcfg; exact instruction-selection differences were not verified in the compiler source.

findings.description: Profile-guided optimization: place a CPU pprof as default.pgo in the main package dir (go build -pgo=auto is default since Go 1.21 for main packages); the compiler uses hot call sites for inlining and (1.22+) interface devirtualization, plus block layout. Official numbers: ~2-14% CPU improvement for typical server workloads, with build time overhead and a modest binary size increase. The profile must represent the real workload (relay + crypto + DNS + rule matching on router traffic); a profile collected on amd64 desktop helps cross-arch builds only approximately (profile is by function/line, so it is architecture-independent in principle). Not yet applied to mihomo; needs a representative profile (pprof endpoint exists in debug mode: /debug/pprof).
findings.technical_details: go.dev/doc/pgo; mihomo exposes net/http middleware.Profiler under /debug when log level is debug (fork:hub/route/server.go:104-115). PGO does not shrink memory; it may enlarge text through inlining (binary +few %). Expected benefit on a router is limited because hot code is in non-PGO'd assembly or crypto/syscalls. Recommend: low priority; only after throughput benchmarks.

findings.topic: Per-connection cost model for mihomo relay
findings.description: A relayed TCP flow in mihomo costs: 2 goroutines (Relay spawns one, caller is the other), 2 sockets (client + upstream), plus protocol goroutines in the outbound (TLS/WebSocket/mux readers), plus a pooled buffer per read in flight (16-32 KiB), plus tunnel metadata, DNS mapping, statistics tracker. The default stats tracker and per-connection context are in tunnel/ (not examined in detail).
findings.technical_details: fork:common/net/sing.go:69-92 Relay; sing bufio.Copy with readWaiter. Goroutine stack growth means TLS-wrapped relays settle at 8-16 KiB stack per goroutine (probable). Order-of-magnitude (hypothesis, not measured on mihomo): 30-60 KB heap per active connection plus kernel socket buffers (not counted in Go RSS), so 1000 conns ~ 30-60 MB; limiting max connections or lowering idle timeouts is a stronger memory knob than GC tuning.

findings.topic: Recommended runtime defaults by RAM class (hypothesis)
findings.description: Table of proposed starting points, all to be validated on real hardware: 64 MB RAM: GOMAXPROCS=1-2 (actual cores), GOGC=50, GOMEMLIMIT=24MiB, build tag with_low_memory, FreeOSMemory every ~5 min when idle, max concurrent conns ~300; 128 MB: GOMAXPROCS=2, GOGC=50-75, GOMEMLIMIT=48MiB, with_low_memory, FreeOSMemory on idle; 256 MB: GOMAXPROCS=min(cores,4), GOGC=100, GOMEMLIMIT=96-128MiB, with_low_memory optional; 512 MB: GOMAXPROCS=cores, GOGC=100, GOMEMLIMIT=192-256MiB (or unset), standard buffers.
findings.technical_details: Rationale: GOMEMLIMIT should leave headroom for kernel (conntrack, nftables, socket buffers) and other daemons (dnsmasq, uhttpd, luci); the ceiling is ~35-45% of RAM for mihomo on low-memory routers. GOGC=50 reduces peak heap by up to ~25% at ~1.3-1.5x GC CPU. These numbers are NOT measured; they derive from the GC guide formulas and the observed amd64 idle RSS (46 MB full build), which implies 64 MB devices cannot run the unpruned build at all. The limit must exceed live heap or the 50% GC CPU limiter engages and performance degrades.

findings.topic: How to set runtime knobs without code changes
findings.description: Runtime tuning can be applied by env vars in the procd init script (GOGC, GOMEMLIMIT, GOMAXPROCS, GODEBUG) or in code with debug.SetGCPercent / debug.SetMemoryLimit / runtime.GOMAXPROCS in main(); mihomo today sets none (main.go only calls maxprocs.Set). GODEBUG can also be embedded at build time via //go:debug directives or go.mod godebug lines (e.g. //go:debug madvdontneed=1, updatemaxprocs=0).
findings.technical_details: runtime GODEBUG options of interest: gctrace=1 (diagnose), madvdontneed, inittrace=1 (init cost), gcshrinkstackoff (disable stack shrinking, runtime/runtime1.go:314), scavtrace. A config-file-driven approach (mihomo YAML key like runtime: {gogc, memory-limit, gomaxprocs}) lets the LuCI/clashwrt wizard pick by detected RAM; hot reload would use debug.SetMemoryLimit(), which is safe at runtime.

findings.description: Go uses all logical CPUs by default; routers are 1-4 cores (MT7621 2c/4t SMT counts as 4 logical CPUs). On SMT cores GOMAXPROCS=4 may add scheduling overhead without proportional throughput. More Ps = more idle spinning threads, per-P mcache and per-P GC worker goroutines, but my experiment shows RSS difference is negligible (4.7 vs 4.8 MB); the real effect is CPU contention with the kernel's softirq/nft work on the same cores.
findings.technical_details: Experiment F005 plus runtime/proc.go GOMAXPROCS logic. A GC cycle uses 25% of GOMAXPROCS as dedicated workers: with P=1 the GC runs fractional/idle workers and steals mutator time; with P=2 half a core. Setting GOMAXPROCS=1 on a 1-core CPU is the default anyway; on 2-4 core routers leaving GOMAXPROCS < cores to keep 1 core for kernel networking is an option (hypothesis).

findings.topic: GOEXPERIMENT and toolchain pinning in CI
findings.description: Upstream CI builds with Go 1.26 for the release matrix (go-version '1.26', and 1.26.0 for another job) while go.mod says 'go 1.20'; runtime GODEBUG defaults therefore follow Go 1.20 semantics (see F001) even on the newest toolchain, so new-version runtime behaviours need explicit //go:debug or go.mod godebug entries. For own builds pin the toolchain (1.26.x or 1.27.x) and record it, since inlining/heap/codegen/size change between versions.
findings.technical_details: fork:.github/workflows/build.yml:167,174,181; the local Go is 1.27.3-X:nodwarf5 (distro build with the nodwarf5 experiment). Newer toolchains tend to grow pclntab and binary slightly. Release process (git tags, SHA-256) in project memory is not affected.

findings.topic: gopacket and other large tables inflate bss/VSZ
findings.description: gopacket/layers allocates 466 KB of heap during init and holds 2.6 MB .bss maps (EthernetTypeMetadata, PPPTypeMetadata), plus errorDecodersForPPPType 0.5 MB; crypto/internal/fips140/drbg.memory is a 32 MiB bss. Bss is not resident until touched, but the init allocations (maps filled in init) are resident. google/pprof/profile adds 154 KB init allocations and exists only for the debug profiler.
findings.technical_details: go tool nm -size -sort size: drbg.memory 33554432 B; gopacket/layers.EthernetTypeMetadata 2621440 B; PPPTypeMetadata 2621440 B. inittrace: gopacket/layers 466192 B, pprof/profile 153840 B. Removing gopacket (used for packet parsing in some listener/outbound like tun/easytier) and pprof behind build tags saves ~0.6 MB init heap and several MB binary; individually small, collectively they define the idle floor.

findings.topic: Linker/compiler facts: no LTO, pclntab, alternatives
findings.description: The gc toolchain has no whole-program/link-time optimization beyond linker deadcode and function-level DCE; pclntab (~1/3 of this binary) is required for stack traces, GC stack maps and panics and cannot be stripped. gccgo is effectively abandoned for current Go versions (stuck far behind the language) and TinyGo targets embedded/WASM with incomplete reflect/net/crypto support; neither can build mihomo (quic-go, gvisor, tailscale, utls). Thus size reduction means removing code, not compiler tricks.
findings.technical_details: Measured .gopclntab = 0x130b815 = 20.1 MB of 61 MB stripped amd64. Statements about gccgo/TinyGo are from project documentation knowledge and were not re-verified by building; classify as probable.

findings.topic: Stack shrinking / per-goroutine stack and TLS cost
findings.description: GC shrinks goroutine stacks that use less than 1/4 of their size (disabled by GODEBUG gcshrinkstackoff); idle goroutines blocked in TLS reads typically keep a 4-8 KiB stack. On busy relays the stack can grow to 16-32 KiB through crypto/tls handshake frames; shrinking happens only at GC, which for a small heap with GOGC=100/4 MiB minimum may be infrequent, so stacks can linger.
findings.technical_details: runtime/runtime1.go:314 gcshrinkstackoff; runtime/stack.go:78 stackMin. A lower GOGC or periodic runtime.GC()/FreeOSMemory (F004) therefore also reclaims stack memory. Magnitude on mihomo not measured.

findings.description: Inbound listener accepts and spawns a goroutine per connection; the protocol is detected by Peek(1) in the mixed listener; the connection is handed to tunnel.HandleTCPConn which runs handleTCPConn synchronously in the listener goroutine. Rule matching runs under configMux.RLock. Dial goes through retry(); relay is N.Relay with one extra goroutine.
findings.technical_details: mixed: Accept loop goroutine (listener/mixed/mixed.go:122-139) -> `go handleConn` per socket (mixed.go:134,148) -> N.NewBufferedConn (bufio.Reader 4096 B, common/net/bufconn.go:18-22) -> socks/http handler -> tunnel.Tunnel.HandleTCPConn (tunnel/tunnel.go:80) -> handleTCPConn (tunnel.go:502): fixMetadata (275), preHandleMetadata (289: fake-ip/redir-host reverse lookup by IP), optional snifferDispatcher.TCPSniff (tunnel.go:~527), peek helper goroutine `go func(){ Peek(1) with 200ms deadline }` only if not yet peeked (tunnel.go:543-552), resolveMetadata (317) -> match (654) iterating getRules(), proxy.DialContext inside retry() with C.DefaultTCPTimeout, statistic.NewTCPTracker (615), handleSocket -> N.Relay (common/net/sing.go:69-92). Relay starts exactly one goroutine (sing.go:76) for the remote->local direction; the calling goroutine does local->remote. Redir/tproxy listeners: `go rl.handleTProxy` per conn (listener/tproxy/tproxy.go:~83); the legacy TCPIn() queue (chan cap 64) also does `go handleTCPConn` (tunnel.go:165-175) but is deprecated. Net per TCP connection: 2 long-lived goroutines (handler+relay copy) + 1 short-lived peek goroutine + the tracker object; outbound adapters (mux, ws, quic streams) add their own goroutines.

findings.description: UDP packets are hashed by NAT key onto a fixed pool of worker goroutines; each new NAT key creates a packetSender and two goroutines.
findings.technical_details: Tunnel.HandleUDPPacket (tunnel.go:99-113) -> initUDP once: numUDPWorkers = max(4, GOMAXPROCS) queues of cap 64 (tunnel.go:85-97,36) -> processUDP -> handleUDPConn (414-500). Packet dropped if queue full. natTable.GetOrCreate(key) (441) creates newPacketSender (tunnel/connection.go:27-39: chan cap 128 = senderCapacity, two maps for destination-NAT mapping, a context). For a new key: `go func(){ dial(); sender.Process(pc, proxy) }` (tunnel.go:489) and inside dial `go handleUDPToLocal(...)` (485) = 2 goroutines per session; handleUDPToLocal loops pc.WaitReadFrom with SetReadDeadline(udpTimeout=60s) (tunnel/connection.go:~150-200, tunnel.go:62). UDP buffers come from common/pool (UDPBufferSize 16 KiB standard / 8 KiB with_low_memory) at the listener (e.g. tproxy/udp.go:69, tproxy/packet.go:102). For tproxy each (remote,local) pair also creates a dedicated transparent UDP socket + reader goroutine (tproxy/packet.go:94-117, nat.GetForLocalConn). Packets queued in a sender hold their pool buffer until processed or dropped.

findings.description: Relay buffer sizes are 32 KiB (TCP) / 16 KiB (UDP) by default and halved by the with_low_memory tag; sing has its own copy of the same constants. DIRECT TCP can bypass user-space buffers via splice.
findings.technical_details: common/pool/buffer_standard.go: RelayBufferSize 32 KiB, UDPBufferSize 16 KiB; buffer_low_memory.go (tag with_low_memory): 16 KiB / 8 KiB. sing v0.5.8 common/buf/buffer_standard.go|buffer_low_memory.go: BufferSize 32/16 KiB, UDPBufferSize 16/8 KiB (the sing buf.Buffer is what bufio.Copy -> CopyExtended actually allocates per direction, bufio/copy.go:100-190).
