Per TCP connection: bufio.Reader 4096 B on the inbound side + up to 2 relay buffers (one per direction, taken from sing buf pool, returned to pool afterwards; pool holds them so steady RSS ~ peak concurrent connections x 2 x BufferSize) + outbound protocol buffers (TLS records, etc.). bufio.Copy first drains BufferedConn.ReadCached, then if both ends unwrap (via UnwrapReader/Upstream: tcpTracker tracker.go:72, BufferedConn bufconn.go:93-100, adapter conn base.go:261) to syscall.Conn it calls copyDirect -> splice(2) with a pipe resized to 1 MiB (sing bufio/splice_linux.go:12-70). Hypothesis: splice applies to DIRECT TCP (raw *net.TCPConn both sides) but not to encrypted outbounds; not exercised here. gVisor/mips stack per-socket TCP buffers: gvisor 20 KiB recv + 20 KiB send (sing-tun stack_gvisor.go:~160-170).

findings.topic: Fake-IP pool: storage and reverse mapping
findings.description: The fake-ip pool is two LRU caches in memory (host->IP and IP->host) with a hard cap of 1000 entries per family, or a bbolt-backed store when profile.store-fake-ip is true. A fake IP is mapped back to a domain in tunnel.preHandleMetadata via resolver.FindHostByIP.
findings.technical_details: component/fakeip/pool.go: Pool{gateway,first,last,offset,cycle,mux,store}; Lookup(host) lowercases, uses store.GetByHost else get() which increments offset, wraps at last (cycle=true) evicting the old IP (pool.go:43-63,105-118). New() (169-196) picks cachefileStore (cache.db) if Persistence else newMemoryStore(options.Size). config.go passes Size: 1000 (config/config.go ~1543-1560). memory.go: lru.LruCache[string,netip.Addr] + lru.LruCache[netip.Addr,string] (memory.go:9-12). Consequence: with more than 1000 distinct domains resolved, the oldest mappings are evicted and any connection to an evicted fake IP fails with 'fake DNS record missing' (tunnel.go:310-311) unless the sniffer recovers a domain (tunnel.go:526-535). Reverse lookup: dns/enhancer.go FindHostByIP (pool.LookBack -> pool6 -> mapping LRU of 4096 for redir-host, enhancer.go:188) called from tunnel.preHandleMetadata (tunnel.go:289-315) which sets metadata.Host, clears DstIP when IsFakeIP (confirmed fake), DNSMode=FakeIP. Pool is cloned on reload (Pool.CloneFrom, pool.go:89-103). RAM is tiny (1000 entries x2 maps); range default 198.18.0.1/16 (config.go).
findings.opus_note: fork:config/config.go:1545 fakeip.Options Size: 1000 (in-memory LRU unless store-fake-ip)

findings.topic: fake-ip-filter modes and what breaks when DNS answers real IPs
findings.description: Three filter modes decide per query name whether to answer with a fake IP or pass to the real resolver; domains that get real IPs lose domain info in the tunnel unless the sniffer or redir-host mapping restores it.
findings.technical_details: Skipper (component/fakeip/skipper.go:20-48): blacklist mode (default FilterBlackList, config.go:536): names matching the filter list get real IPs, everything else fake; whitelist: only matching names get fake IPs; rule mode (fake-ip-filter-mode: rule): ordered rules with action 'fake-ip'/'real-ip' (config.go:1625-1655; rule-sets with behavior domain/classical allowed, only domain rules honoured). Applied in dns/middleware.go:149-190 withFakeIP; also HTTPS/SVCB queries get empty answers under fake-ip (middleware.go:~176). Fallback nameserver hostnames are auto-added to the skip set unless rule mode (config.go:1508-1521). If DNS gives real IPs for a domain: (1) metadata.Host is empty at tunnel entry, so DOMAIN/DOMAIN-SUFFIX/GEOSITE/rule-set(domain) rules cannot match unless the sniffer extracts SNI/Host or MappingEnabled redir-host mapping (enhancer InsertHostByIP, 10s TTL entries, middleware.go:55-75) knows the IP; (2) rules then fall to IP rules after ResolveIP, i.e. policy changes silently (a PROXY domain may match IP-CIDR/GEOIP DIRECT, or MATCH); (3) the real IP in a hosts-less path means the proxy node gets an IP instead of a domain (remote DNS no longer used: DNS leak/geo-mismatch for CDN); (4) shared CDN IPs mean IP->policy is ambiguous. Typical required real-ip set: NTP, STUN, captive portals, LAN domains, game/VoIP domains, proxy-server hostnames (DNS dialer), domains in a kernel bypass set. This is the core constraint for an IP-level safe bypass: a bypass keyed only by destination IP cannot represent domain-specific policy.

findings.description: Sniffer runs inside handleTCPConn before rule matching and can rescue a failed fake-IP lookup; nameserver-policy is a per-domain resolver selection implemented as DomainTrie/rule policies inside the DNS Resolver.
findings.technical_details: tunnel.go:522-540: if sniffing enabled, TCPSniff (component/sniffer/dispatcher.go:122-167) is tried after the lookup; success clears preHandleFailed. replaceDomain (dispatcher.go:169-181) sets metadata.Host and optionally overrides DstIP (override-destination). Sniffers: TLS, HTTP, QUIC (quic_sniffer.go is 19.7 KB, large table) with sniff failure cache (dispatcher.go:301-320, 'bitmap' structure). For UDP: DoSniff happens inside the dial closure (tunnel.go:446-452) via UDPSniff (dispatcher.go:85-120). Sniffer delays the first byte (wait for ClientHello) which is also why the peek helper exists. nameserver-policy: dns/resolver.go dnsPolicy list built by makePolicy (resolver.go:568-600) from a trie (domainTriePolicy) / geosite / rule-set matchers; matchPolicy (resolver.go:261-275) is consulted at the start of ExchangeContext (215, 300) before main/fallback; DirectFollowPolicy and ProxyServerPolicy are separate policy sets (resolver.go:465-483). A policy hit routes the query to its own nameserver list (possibly via a proxy group), bypassing fallback logic.

findings.description: Four TUN stacks: mips (pure-Go mipstack, the fork's config default), system (kernel TCP via local listener + packet NAT), gvisor (gVisor netstack, needs with_gvisor), mixed (system TCP + gvisor UDP, needs with_gvisor).
findings.technical_details: Selection: sing-tun stack.go:41-63 (""|mips -> NewMipstack; gvisor -> NewGVisor; mixed -> NewMixed; system -> NewSystem). Default in mihomo config: Stack: C.TunMips (config/config.go:548); enum constant/tun.go:16-19. System: stack_system.go (996 lines): reads TUN with tunLoop/batchLoopLinux (batchSize buffers each mtu+headroom, stack_system.go:190-260), rewrites addresses (NAT tables stack_system_nat.go) so the kernel TCP stack terminates the flow on a local TCPListener (tcp4/tcp6, lines 136-176, acceptLoop per family); UDP handled in userspace with own NAT. Cheapest RAM and best TCP throughput (kernel TCP, no user TCP state machine), no extra dependency. gVisor: stack_gvisor.go sets TCP buffers 20 KiB recv/send per connection (line ~160), full user-space TCP -> highest CPU/RAM per flow, pulls github.com/metacubex/gvisor (324 files in go list -deps) and is also required by tailscale, wireguard device (mipstack used in wireguard.go), and with_gvisor tag. Mixed: embeds *System and replaces only UDP forwarder with gvisor (stack_mixed.go:17-46). Mipstack: 41,202 lines pure Go (incl. BBR/CUBIC/Reno, fragment, IPv6) with no with_gvisor requirement; per-conn buffers unverified. Costs are qualitative here; no throughput numbers were measured (hypothesis for ranking: system < mixed < mips ~ gvisor in CPU per byte for TCP).

findings.description: auto-redirect creates an nftables table 'mihomo' (inet) with REDIRECT/mark rules and a local redirect server; route-address-set and route-exclude-address-set are rule-providers (behavior ipcidr) converted to netipx.IPSet and loaded into nftables interval sets. Only the nftables backend supports them.
findings.technical_details: listener/sing_tun/server.go:431-476: auto-redirect requires auto-route; tun.NewAutoRedirect(TableName 'mihomo', DisableNFTables from env DISABLE_NFTABLES, RouteAddressSet/RouteExcludeAddressSet pointers); each name in route-address-set / route-exclude-address-set must be an existing rule-provider (error otherwise), loaded by updateRule (server.go:574-603) that requires the strategy to implement ToIpCidr() (ipcidr_strategy.go:~108 ToIpCidr -> *netipx.IPSet). Any set sets AutoRedirectMarkMode (route marks/ output mark 'AutoRedirectOutputMark', also forces a global dialer routing-mark, server.go:~519-530). On provider update, updateRule(..., update=true) calls autoRedirect.UpdateRouteAddressSet() (server.go:600) -> nftablesUpdateRouteAddressSet (sing-tun redirect_nftables.go:316-331) which re-creates sets inet4/6_route_address_set and inet4/6_route_exclude_address_set (redirect_nftables_rules.go:32-62) via nftablesCreateIPSet (redirect_nftables_exprs.go:130-180) as interval sets (From + IntervalEnd elements) through github.com/metacubex/nftables netlink. Chains: output mangle priority, prerouting at NATDest+1/+2 (redirect_nftables.go:59-149). iptables backend: UpdateRouteAddressSet is a no-op (redirect_linux.go:157-165 checks useNFTables) and redirect_iptables.go has no set support. On OpenWrt with fw4 the library writes /etc/nftables.d/0-mihomo-auto-redirect.nft accepting tun traffic in input/forward and runs `fw4 reload` (redirect_nftables_rules_openwrt.go:15-52). Memory: IPSet is kept in mihomo (ranges slice) plus the kernel set. This is the existing, in-tree template for dynamic nft set maintenance, but it is a static provider->set mapping, not a per-connection decision cache.

findings.topic: TPROXY listener (TCP and UDP) and redir
findings.description: TPROXY is a plain transparent TCP listener plus an IP_TRANSPARENT UDP socket with per-flow reply sockets; mihomo does not by default install firewall rules for it (helper for iptables exists).
findings.technical_details: TCP: listener/tproxy/tproxy.go New(): net.ListenConfig with MPTCP forced off (tproxy.go ~60-65), setsockopt IP_TRANSPARENT (setsockopt_linux.go), accept loop -> go handleTProxy: the original destination is just conn.LocalAddr() (tproxy.go:~36-44) then tunnel.HandleTCPConn(inbound.NewSocket(target, conn, C.TPROXY)). UDP: tproxy/udp.go:~60-90: one IP_TRANSPARENT UDP socket, a single reader goroutine allocating pool.Get(UDPBufferSize)(16 KiB) per datagram and a 1024-byte OOB buffer, ReadMsgUDPAddrPort + getOrigDst/getDSCP from cmsg (udp_linux.go:99-165); replies: createOrGetLocalConn/listenLocalConn (packet.go:55-117) dial a transparent socket bound to the original destination (udp_linux.go dialUDP :23-70) and spawn one reader goroutine per (src,dst) pair, closed via natTable.RangeForLocalConn when the session ends (connection.go closeAllLocalCoon). Redir TCP (listener/redir/tcp_linux.go) gets original dst by SO_ORIGINAL_DST (conntrack). tproxy_iptables.go has SetTProxyIPTables (uses `iptables` CLI via common/cmd, mark 0x2d0 / table 0x2d0, with a bypass list) - legacy helper, not nftables. In clashwrt the rules are set up externally, so none of this is needed.

findings.topic: Rule engine: types and which metadata each needs
findings.description: Rules are evaluated linearly in order under configMux.RLock; helper callbacks lazily resolve DNS and process. Only a subset depends solely on destination IP/port/network.
findings.technical_details: Parser: rules/parser.go:12-100 types: DOMAIN, DOMAIN-SUFFIX, DOMAIN-KEYWORD, DOMAIN-REGEX, DOMAIN-WILDCARD, GEOSITE (need metadata.Host / RuleHost()); GEOIP, IP-CIDR(6), IP-SUFFIX, IP-ASN (DstIP; call helper.ResolveIP() unless 'no-resolve', ipcidr.go:38-48, geoip.go:35-48 - resolving fills DstIP via DNS from Host, tunnel.go:333-348); SRC-GEOIP, SRC-IP-CIDR, SRC-IP-SUFFIX, SRC-IP-ASN (SrcIP), SRC-PORT, DST-PORT, IN-PORT, DSCP, NETWORK, UID, IN-TYPE, IN-USER, IN-NAME (inbound/user metadata), PROCESS-NAME/PATH/*-REGEX/*-WILDCARD (helper.FindProcess -> netlink + /proc scan, F021), REMATCH-NAME, SUB-RULE, AND/OR/NOT, RULE-SET (domain/ipcidr/classical providers), MATCH. Also a rule action can be Pass or Rematch (tunnel.go:668-690). A rule-set with behavior ipcidr is pure destination-IP; behavior domain is host-only; classical can contain anything. A connection can be bypassed at IP level safely only when every rule evaluated before the first match is one of: IP-CIDR/GEOIP/IP-ASN/DST-PORT/NETWORK/MATCH/SRC-IP-* (SRC is available at kernel level as source address) and the DstIP is real (not fake-IP); anything depending on Host, process, UID, IN-NAME/IN-USER, DSCP (visible in kernel but not in same form) or logic composites containing them makes the decision connection-specific. Under fake-IP the DstIP is cleared (tunnel.go:296-300) and the decision is domain-based, so the kernel only sees the real IP after mihomo (or the dialer) resolves it.

findings.description: Providers have behavior domain/ipcidr/classical and format yaml/text/mrs. Domain sets are a succinct trie (DomainSet), IP sets are a sorted netipx.IPRange slice; classical keeps one rule object per line.
findings.technical_details: Strategies: rules/provider/provider.go:156-172. domainStrategy -> trie.DomainSet (component/trie/domain_set.go:20-24: leaves, labelBitmap []uint64, labels []byte, ranks, selects []int32 built by bitmap.IndexSelect32R64, domain_set.go:312-314; very compact, reversed-key sorted build via DomainSetBuilder.keys []string which holds ALL strings until Build). ipcidrStrategy -> cidr.IpCidrSet{rr []netipx.IPRange} reused as *netipx.IPSet by unsafe cast (component/cidr/ipcidr_set.go:12-76); Merge() goes through netipx.IPSetBuilder (extra copy) for yaml/text; IsContain is a binary search over ranges (O(log n)). classicalStrategy: slice of full C.Rule objects (parsed per line, rules/provider/classical_strategy.go) - heaviest per entry. The fork go.mod also has metacubex/bart (rules/common or ipasn use), but ipcidr rule-sets use the range slice not bart. .mrs = zstd stream: magic 'MRS\x01', behavior byte, int64 count, int64 extra length, then FromMrs (rules/provider/mrs_reader.go:15-77). Text/yaml parse line by line; yaml parses each line with yaml.Unmarshal into a RulePayload (provider.go:215-250) which is far slower and more garbage-prone than text. Loading: component/resource/fetcher.go Initial() does os.ReadFile of the whole file, MakeHash md5 of whole buffer, then parser (fetcher.go:56-67,129-168); file bytes are retained until the parser returns.

findings.topic: Likely cause of the ~42 MB transient startup spike
findings.description: Candidates ranked by evidence: (1) all rule-providers load concurrently on arm64/amd64; (2) per-element binary.Read allocations plus whole-file ReadFile and zstd decoder buffers; (3) NewDomainStrategy builder / IPSetBuilder copies for non-mrs formats. None measured; the previous gctrace (heap 8-9 MB live, ~42 MB peak for ~0.1 s) is consistent with garbage rather than retained structures.
findings.technical_details: (1) hub/executor/concurrent_load_unlimit.go has tag `386 || amd64 || arm64 || arm64be` and sets concurrentCount = math.MaxInt; loadProvider (hub/executor/executor.go:317-353) therefore starts one goroutine per provider with an effectively unlimited semaphore. mips/mipsle use concurrentCount=1; other archs (arm, etc.) 5. The BPI-R4 (arm64) thus parses every provider at the same time, and each holds raw file bytes + zstd decoder + decoded structure simultaneously. (2) rules/provider/mrs_reader.go creates klauspost zstd.NewReader (streaming, default concurrency and window buffers) per provider; trie.ReadDomainSetBin (component/trie/domain_set_bin.go:53-113) and cidr.ReadIpCidrSet (cidr/ipcidr_set_bin.go:38-77) call encoding/binary.Read once per uint64 / twice per range with 16-byte arrays; Go's binary.Read heap-allocates `bs := make([]byte, n)` on every call (go:encoding/binary/binary.go:258-263), i.e. millions of 8-16 B garbage objects for large sets (only collected at the next GC; with GOGC=50 and GOMEMLIMIT=48MiB this shows as the spike). (3) resource.Fetcher keeps the file buffer plus md5 hashing plus parser output alive during parse. Verification plan for the main agent: run with GODEBUG=gctrace=1 and (a) concurrency forced to 1, (b) a build where ReadDomainSetBin/ReadIpCidrSet read the whole slice with one io.ReadFull + binary.BigEndian.Uint64 decode, (c) zstd.NewReader(..., zstd.WithDecoderConcurrency(1), zstd.WithDecoderMaxWindow(...)). Cheapest fix candidate: make concurrentCount 1 (or 2) under a new tag or for all (isolated file swap), then batch-read in the mrs readers.
findings.opus_note: Concurrency part confirmed: hub/executor/concurrent_load_unlimit.go concurrentCount=MaxInt on 386/amd64/arm64/arm64be; _single.go =1 on mips/mipsle; _limit.go =5 elsewhere. Spike attribution still a hypothesis until gctrace with concurrency 1 on BPI-R4.

findings.topic: Protocol registration points and rebase-friendly per-protocol tagging
findings.description: Outbounds are registered by one switch in adapter/parser.go (ParseProxy), inbounds by one switch in listener/parse.go; adapter constructors live in adapter/outbound/<proto>.go and transports in transport/<proto>. The stub-file pattern already used for tailscale/zerotier/easytier gives minimal-diff tags.
findings.technical_details: adapter/parser.go:30-219: case ss, ssr, socks5, http, vmess, vless, snell, trojan, hysteria, hysteria2, wireguard, tuic, shadowquic, gost-relay, direct, dns, reject, rematch, ssh, mieru, anytls, sudoku, masque, trusttunnel, openvpn, tailscale, zerotier, easytier. Each case decodes into outbound.<X>Option then calls outbound.New<X>. listener/parse.go:23-171: socks, http, tproxy, redir, mixed, tunnel, tun, shadowsocks, snell, vmess, vless, trojan, hysteria2, hysteria2-realm, tuic, shadowquic, anytls, mieru, sudoku, trusttunnel. Config-level parsing of proxy-groups, providers and listeners goes through the same constructors. Minimal-diff scheme: for each heavy protocol X add `<x>_stub.go` (`//go:build no_X`) in adapter/outbound defining the Option struct (same fields, needed by the structure decoder) and `NewX` returning an error 'disabled by no_X', and add `//go:build !no_X` to the real file - zero edits to parser.go; same for listener packages (listener/<x>/ stub exporting New returning error, and in listener/inbound/<x>.go constructors which must still compile: each listener has inbound/<x>.go in listener/inbound that imports the real implementation, so that file needs the same stub treatment). Option structs shared with other code (e.g. outbound.<X>Option referenced in listener/config or transport shared structs) are the rebase-risk points; keep stubs a verbatim copy of the Option struct. Transports shared by several protocols (transport/vless, vmess, gun, xhttp, kcptun, mkcp, shadowtls, restls, reality, tlsmirror, jls) require checking VLESS/VMess/Trojan wiring (vless.go imports quic-go for XHTTP/H3; http.go/trojan.go/vmess.go import metacubex/http+tls) - those are compile-time linked and cannot be tagged out cheaply without editing the protocol file itself (invasive).

findings.description: Every connection and UDP session is registered in a global sync.Map with a UUID and metadata clone; byte counters are atomics; a 1 Hz ticker computes speeds. API reads iterate the whole map.
findings.technical_details: statistic.NewTCPTracker (tracker.go:119-152) creates TrackerInfo{UUID, Metadata, atomic counters, Start, Chain, ProviderChain, Rule, RulePayload} (strings built per connection) and manager.Join -> m.connections.Store(c.ID() /*uuid string*/) (manager.go:40-42). Close() leaves; Snapshot() (manager.go:84-97) copies all TrackerInfo pointers for /connections (JSON). Per read/write: two atomic adds (PushUploaded/PushDownloaded + per-conn totals; tracker.go:50-70). A single goroutine ticks every 1 s (manager.go:116-122). Memory read (manager.updateMemory -> memory.GetMemoryInfo) only when the API asks. Costs scale with live connections (every long-lived flow: tens of KB with strings, chain slices, metadata clone); disabling would need a build tag around NewTCPTracker/NewUDPTracker call sites (tunnel.go:479,615), but the traffic API (/traffic, /connections) would then be empty.

findings.description: Log events go through an unbuffered channel to an observable with per-subscriber goroutines; per-connection INFO log lines (logMetadata) are formatted for every connection.
findings.technical_details: log/log.go:13-14 logCh = make(chan Event) feeding observable.NewObservable[Event]; producers at lines 39-57 block until the observable goroutine takes the event. Subscribers: API /logs websockets. tunnel.logMetadata (tunnel.go:635-652) formats every successful connection at info level (string building + Printf even when level filtered? the level check is inside log package; Event is allocated first - hypothesis). Reducing cost: log-level warning/silent in production; or build-time constant. SingLogger bridge: log/sing.go.

findings.description: cache.db is a bbolt file opened at startup (selected proxies, fake-ip state, rule/proxy cache); geodata loads whole files unless a memory-conservative loader is selected (default); mmdb opened via maxminddb.

findings.description: Process lookup runs only when a process rule is evaluated (find-process-mode strict) or when mode=always; it uses sock_diag netlink for uid+inode, then scans /proc/<pid>/fd for the inode.
findings.technical_details: tunnel.go:351-375 FindProcess helper (once per connection); FindProcessMode: strict (default; lazily on first process rule), always, off (tunnel.go:395-402; component/process/find_process_mode.go). component/process/process_linux.go:65-92: findProcessName -> resolveSocketByNetlink (93-175, sock_diag by src IP/port), fallback resolveSocketByProcFS (293-352, parses /proc/net/{tcp,udp}[6] text, linear in table size); resolveProcessNameByProcSearch (177-235): os.ReadDir("/proc"), for every numeric pid ReadDir /proc/<pid>/fd and Readlink each fd until socket:[inode] matches: O(processes x open fds) syscalls per new connection; resolveProcessNameByUID (236-272) similar. On a router running dnsmasq/mihomo/uhttpd (tens of pids) this is cheap per lookup, but with process rules on a TUN with thousands of connections/s it burns CPU. Not useful for transparent-proxy traffic from LAN clients (source processes are on other machines): the lookup only finds local-process sockets. For a router profile the whole feature can be turned off with find-process-mode: off, or removed with a tag around the FindProcess callback.

findings.topic: Runtime parameters: GOMAXPROCS and worker counts
findings.description: automaxprocs is applied at start; UDP worker count follows GOMAXPROCS (min 4); channel capacities are fixed.
findings.technical_details: main.go imports go.uber.org/automaxprocs/maxprocs (main.go:31) to honor cgroup CPU limits; tunnel.initUDP uses max(4, GOMAXPROCS) workers (tunnel.go:85-97); queueCapacity 64, senderCapacity 128 (tunnel.go:36-37). No GC tuning in main.go (grep of debug./GOGC in main.go and executor found none); clashwrt sets GOGC=50 and GOMEMLIMIT=48MiB externally. Each of the up-to-N UDP worker queues holds C.PacketAdapter pointers that pin 16 KiB pool buffers (queue cap 64 x workers) so worst-case pinned UDP memory is workers x 64 x 16 KiB = 4 MiB at 4 workers (8 KiB halves it) plus 128 x 16 KiB per active sender.

findings.topic: DNS server and resolver structure relevant to routers
findings.description: The DNS server is an in-process miekg/dns server with middleware chain (hosts, fake-ip, resolver) and an LRU cache; fake-ip responses carry TTL fakeIPTTL; real queries go through resolver with nameserver/fallback/policy and optional DoH/DoT/DoQ clients (quic-go).
findings.technical_details: dns/middleware.go:240-241 builds the chain: withHosts -> withMapping (redir-host) or withFakeIP -> withResolver; the fake-ip answer has Authoritative=true, RA=true, TTL = dns.fake-ip-ttl (middleware.go:188-195). Fake-IP TTL influences how long clients cache a mapping vs pool eviction at 1000 entries (F004). DoQ/DoH3 clients link quic-go even if unused. Fallback + nameserver-policy + proxy-server-nameserver exist to avoid proxy-resolution loops (dns/resolver.go:465-483). IPv6: AAAA under fake-ip returns empty unless fake-ip-range6 set (middleware.go:~164-168).

findings.description: Proposed split based on code coupling, to be validated by builds.
findings.technical_details: Ultra Lightweight (router, transparent proxy via tproxy/redir/mixed, rule-sets .mrs, small config): exclude via tags (existing) no_tailscale no_zerotier no_easytier no_fake_tcp with_low_memory; no with_gvisor unless tun gvisor/mixed needed (default mips stack is fine) - note tailscale is gated by with_gvisor so dropping with_gvisor also drops tailscale; new tags to add: quic family (hysteria, hysteria2, tuic, masque, shadowquic; keep only if user needs), jls/restls/shadowtls, ssh, openvpn, mieru, sudoku, kcp/mkcp, wireguard/amneziawg, trusttunnel, gost-relay, ssr/snell, geodata (GEOSITE/GEOIP via .dat) with mmdb only, external-ui updater and core self-upgrade, pprof/debug route, sniffer QUIC. Keep: ss/ss2022, vmess/vless(+reality/xtls vision), trojan, socks5/http, direct/reject, anytls (if small), mixed/redir/tproxy listeners, DNS (fake-ip). Lightweight (Router): as Ultra plus quic (hysteria2/tuic), wireguard, ssh; with_low_memory. Performance: with_gvisor optional (TUN mixed/system), full quic family, all transports; keep tailscale/zerotier/easytier off anyway, 128-bit buffer sizes standard, concurrent provider load limited to 1-2. Options not needing code changes: find-process-mode off, log-level warning, external-controller off or unix socket, geodata-mode, profile.store-cache only if needed.

findings.topic: What not to touch without architecture changes
findings.description: Core invariants that make mihomo correct: metadata normalization, fake-IP reverse mapping, rule matching under configMux, retry/dial, tracker/relay pairing, NAT table semantics for UDP, and hot reload cloning of pools.
findings.technical_details: Do not alter without redesign: tunnel.preHandleMetadata and resolver.FindHostByIP (domain recovery, tunnel.go:289-315); the rule evaluation order + helper lazy callbacks (tunnel.go:317-412,654-711); rematch/pass semantics (668-690); packetSender / natTable / writeBack pairing for UDP (tunnel/connection.go, tproxy nat); DNS hijack interplay (listener/sing_tun/dns.go) and system DNS blacklist (server.go ~ 'AddSystemDnsBlacklist'); reload path executor.ApplyConfig (Pool.CloneFrom keeps fake-ip range stable, enhancer.PatchFrom); dialer.DefaultRoutingMark/interface binding used with auto-redirect mark mode (server.go:519-530) because direct outbound dials are marked to bypass the redirect rules. Any kernel bypass must be invalidated on rule/proxy/provider update (tunnel.UpdateRules sets rules atomically under configMux) and on fake-ip flush.

findings.description: Both directions are copied by two goroutines calling sing bufio.Copy; the fork's Relay is a lighter bufio.CopyConn (no task.Group/context). One goroutine pair per connection.
findings.technical_details: tunnel handleSocket -> N.Relay (fork:common/net/sing.go:69-92): spawns one goroutine for dst->src, runs src->dst in the caller, closeWrite on EOF. Called from fork:tunnel/connection.go:220.

findings.topic: Splice decision logic in sing Copy
findings.description: bufio.Copy unwraps wrappers (UnwrapCountReader/Writer follow Upstream/UnwrapReader and turn the statistics tracker into CountFuncs), drains N.CachedReader (BufferedConn bufio buffer) first, then if BOTH ends are syscall.Conn calls copyDirect -> splice(2) via a pipe. Otherwise falls to CopyExtended: ReadWaiter (WaitReadBuffer, zero extra copy) if available, else pooled ReadBuffer/WriteBuffer loop.
findings.technical_details: Loop at sing copy.go:28-81 (max 10 CopyExtendedOnce replaceable-unwrap rounds); syscall.Conn check copy.go:68-77; ReadWaiter path copy.go:~96-115; pool fallback CopyExtendedWithPool copy.go:159-190. splice implementation: 1 MiB F_SETPIPE_SZ pipe per direction per connection (pipe2 + 2 splice per chunk, SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK|MOVE), counters invoked per chunk. Counting is therefore kept even on the splice path (traffic statistics do NOT force a userspace copy).

findings.topic: EXPERIMENT: DIRECT CONNECT tunnel uses splice
findings.description: Built fork (go 1.27.3, amd64) with config mixed-port + MATCH,DIRECT on loopback, ran under gdb with catch syscall counting (strace is absent), 20 MB transfer via curl -p (HTTP CONNECT tunnel). Result: splice entered/returned 94 stops (~47 calls, ~0.4 MB/call), pipe2 4 stops (1 per direction), only ~30 write stops -> data path is splice, zero-copy in userspace.
findings.technical_details: Counts are catchpoint hits (entry+exit each). Same 20 MB transferred as plain HTTP proxy request (no CONNECT, curl without -p): splice 0, pipe2 0, ~1360 write stops (~680 write calls) and ~1384 read calls -> userspace copy, because the HTTP listener handles each plain-HTTP request itself (HTTP transport + io.Copy), not the tunnel relay. Not measured: throughput/CPU, arm/mips behaviour, TLS destinations (CONNECT to :443 is same path), tun inbound.

findings.topic: Conditions that defeat splice (fallback to userspace)
findings.description: (1) Either side not a raw *net.TCPConn after unwrapping: any outbound protocol with its own framing/crypto (ss, vmess, vless, trojan, TLS, REALITY, ws, grpc, h2) -> never splice, uses ReadWaiter/pool path with encryption in userspace; only DIRECT and plain tunnels (and maybe http/socks5 upstream without TLS) qualify. (2) Inbound from TUN: gvisor/mipstack TCPConn are not syscall.Conn (adapter/outbound/base.go:286-289 even special-cases ipstackConn) -> userspace copy through the netstack. system stack gives real kernel sockets (loopback to its own listener) and can splice. (3) Pending cached bytes in BufferedConn/sniffer peek are written first (copy.go:36-52), then splice continues (ReaderReplaceable false only while buffered>0). (4) NewDeadlineConn wrapping of non-syscall conns in outbound.NewConn (base.go:284-296) is a userspace wrapper. (5) Plain HTTP proxy requests (non-CONNECT) never reach the relay.
findings.technical_details: The sniffer path writes the peeked bytes to remoteConn then calls handleSocket (fork:tunnel/tunnel.go:~595-623), so sniffing does not disable splice for DIRECT after the first bytes (inferred from code and the experiment, sniffer was off in the test; not experimentally verified with sniffer on).

findings.topic: Splice memory/CPU trade on weak routers
findings.description: Splice removes two copies per chunk and Go-heap buffers (no 16/32 KiB pool buffers per direction) but costs per-connection pipe2 and up to 1 MiB pipe capacity per direction (pages allocated lazily by kernel, charged to the user pipe-user-pages-soft limit 16384 pages by default) and 3 syscalls per chunk (splice-in, splice-out, plus epoll wake) vs 2 (read+write) for the copy path.
findings.technical_details: Page-lazy allocation means idle connections cost little, but 1 MiB F_SETPIPE_SZ lets one hot flow queue 1 MiB kernel memory; on 64-128 MB routers with many bulk flows this is a RAM risk. Whether splice is a net CPU win on MIPS (memcpy-bound at ~100-300 MB/s) is plausible but not measured here.
findings.opus_note: fact part confirmed: sing splice_linux.go:12,24 sets F_SETPIPE_SZ=1 MiB per pipe (Go stdlib internal/poll/splice_linux.go does the same). Memory impact on routers remains a hypothesis to measure.

findings.description: Relay buffers are pooled: 32 KiB TCP / 16 KiB UDP by default; with build tag with_low_memory 16 KiB / 8 KiB and common.LowMemory=true makes Copy prefer the copyWaitWithPool path even when needCopy. Fork go.mod pins sing v0.5.8; the tag is a free profile knob for Ultra/Lightweight.
findings.technical_details: buffer_standard.go:6-7, buffer_low_memory.go:6-7 (//go:build with_low_memory), low_memory.go:5 / low_memory_stub.go:5, copy.go:96-110. Socket buffers: mihomo does not set SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF on relay sockets by default (grep of component/dialer found nothing) -> kernel autotuning (tcp_rmem/wmem) applies.

findings.topic: Go runtime GC knobs not set
findings.description: Fork main.go sets no GOGC/GOMEMLIMIT/SetGCPercent (grep empty); memory behaviour is entirely left to env. For a 10-20 MB RSS target a default GOGC=100 can double heap; setting GOMEMLIMIT/GOGC=50 or debug.SetGCPercent at start is the cheapest runtime lever.
findings.technical_details: Trade-off: lower GOGC raises GC CPU on weak cores. Needs measurement on target; belongs partly to the memory agent.

findings.description: Per-packet cost: inbound socks/mixed/tproxy UDP listener reads one datagram per syscall (WaitReadFrom), pushes through a channel into one of max(4,GOMAXPROCS) hash-sharded worker queues (cap 64), then pc.WriteTo (sendto) to the upstream; reverse direction in a goroutine per NAT entry doing WaitReadFrom + WriteBack. Roughly 1 recvfrom + 1 sendto + channel handoff + 2 goroutine switches per packet. No recvmmsg/sendmmsg anywhere in the fork or sing paths for plain UDP (grep for ReadBatch/WriteBatch in fork returned nothing).
findings.technical_details: fork:tunnel/tunnel.go:86-111 (udpQueues), fork:tunnel/connection.go:154-193, fork:listener/socks/udp.go:65. Cost estimate is hypothesis; weak CPUs are dominated by syscall + goroutine wake per packet at small-packet rates (DNS/QUIC/games).

findings.description: quic-go fork (v0.61.1) uses ipv4.PacketConn/ipv6 ReadBatch (recvmmsg) in sys_conn_oob.go and UDP GSO (UDP_SEGMENT) when kernel supports it; GSO can be switched off via env QUIC_GO_DISABLE_GSO and the fork has a QUICGoDisableGSO config. This only affects QUIC-based outbounds (hysteria/hysteria2/tuic/masque), not the generic UDP relay. x/net v0.35.0 (go.mod) provides ipv4.PacketConn.ReadBatch/WriteBatch on Linux (recvmmsg/sendmmsg).
findings.technical_details: sys_conn_oob.go:36,149,173,249-252; sys_conn_helper_linux.go:63-69. GSO may need UDP_SEGMENT-capable NIC path; software GSO in 6.12 is OK for loopback/veth but gains on MIPS Ethernet with no HW offload are mostly fewer syscalls, not fewer packets.

findings.description: sing-tun v0.4.28 stacks: mipstack (default when stack empty), gvisor, system, mixed. Linux TUN supports IFF_VNET_HDR + TSO/GRO/USO (GSO option) with batch read/write (BatchRead, up to idealBatchSize 128), GRO tables for TCP and UDP, checksum offload toggles; mihomo exposes tun.gso and tun.gso-max-size (default 65536). Stack System reads batches and rewrites packets in-place to NAT TCP to a local listener (kernel TCP does the rest, splice-capable); Mixed = system for TCP, gvisor for UDP; mipstack/gvisor terminate TCP in a userspace netstack (copy per packet, userspace TCP state, more RAM).
findings.technical_details: tun_linux.go:52,121-145,173-240,290,334,422-440; tun_offload.go:12-16; tun_offload_linux.go:44 (GSOUDPL4); stack_system.go:189,251 (BatchRead); stack.go:41-63; fork listener/config/tun.go:22-23, listener/sing_tun/server.go:145,396. Kernel: IFF_VNET_HDR/TSO since ~2.6.x, TUN UDP GSO (USO) needs >=6.2, OpenWrt 25.12 kernel 6.12 qualifies; TUN GRO requires TUNSETOFFLOAD ioctl. With GSO the userspace sees up to 64 KiB super-packets: fewer syscalls and fewer per-packet stack traversals (the dominant TUN cost), but needs enough RAM for 64 KiB * batch buffers (hypothesis: raises RSS by a few MB) and kmod-tun.

findings.topic: TUN vs transparent proxy (redirect/tproxy) on routers
findings.description: For a router, TUN (any stack) is structurally more expensive than REDIRECT/TPROXY because every forwarded packet crosses userspace twice; redirect/tproxy hand mihomo real TCP sockets (splice-capable) and skip the TUN packet path entirely. sing-tun also ships auto-redirect (nftables) code.
findings.technical_details: redirect_nftables*.go, redirect_linux.go in sing-tun. This is the dominant architecture lever for throughput on weak routers, bigger than any micro-optimisation. Not measured here.

findings.description: OpenWrt 6.12 generic config has CONFIG_IO_URING disabled; Go stdlib has no io_uring netpoll; third-party Go io_uring libs need cgo-free raw syscalls, per-ring memory, and are blocked on seccomp/old kernels. Gains over epoll are modest for 1-socket-per-goroutine workloads, and 32-bit MIPS/ARMv7 io_uring support is weak.
findings.technical_details: openwrt:target/linux/generic/config-6.12:2851 '# CONFIG_IO_URING is not set'. Enabling needs a custom kernel (not user-installable as a kmod).

findings.description: AF_XDP: CONFIG_XDP_SOCKETS not set in OpenWrt generic config; also needs driver XDP support and bypasses netfilter/routing, useless for a terminating proxy that must maintain real TCP sockets. MSG_ZEROCOPY: helps only for large (>~10 KB) sends and adds completion handling via the error queue; Go net does not expose it; loses on loopback and small chunks. sendfile: irrelevant (no file source); splice already covers socket-to-socket.
findings.technical_details: openwrt config-6.12:7721 '# CONFIG_XDP_SOCKETS is not set'. kernel doc: Documentation/networking/msg_zerocopy.rst.

findings.description: sing-box common/ktls implements Linux kernel TLS (TCP_ULP 'tls', TLS_TX/TLS_RX) for TLS 1.3 only, AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, by hooking crypto/tls internals via //go:linkname (build tag linux && go1.25 && badlinkname, needs -checklinkname=0-style flags). With RX offload it can splice from the TLS socket. Requires kernel with CONFIG_TLS and TLS1.3 support.
findings.technical_details: ktls.go:1 (build tag), ktls_linux.go:114-139 (Load/setupKernel: support.TLS && TLS_Version13 required), ktls_cipher_suites_linux.go:40-45 (chacha), ktls_read.go splice RX pending. OpenWrt: CONFIG_TLS is '# not set' in generic config-6.12:6769; available only as kmod-tls (netsupport.mk:1077). Applicability: only to stacks using stdlib crypto/tls with TLS1.3 (trojan, vless-tls, plain tls); mihomo mostly uses metacubex/utls and REALITY which do not go through stdlib state. On MIPS/ARMv7 without crypto engine kernel AES/ChaCha is not cheaper than Go's; benefit is only the removed copies and ability to splice plaintext<->kTLS socket (inbound TCP -> outbound TLS), which could allow TLS-proxy relay zero-copy. Treated as low value for the target, high fragility.

findings.topic: Hardware flow offload not available generically
findings.description: CONFIG_NF_FLOW_TABLE is not set in OpenWrt generic config (enabled per-target / kmod-nf-flow); BBR also not set. Fast path for DIRECT traffic therefore competes with (and the project can reuse) kernel flow offload rather than mihomo user-space splice, which relates to the project key question (out of this agent's scope).
findings.technical_details: openwrt config-6.12:4390, 6626.

findings.description: Each relayed TCP connection costs 2 goroutines (relay pair) + handler goroutine; Go starts goroutines at 2-8 KiB stacks (grows to 32 KiB+ in TLS/crypto paths), pooled 16-32 KiB buffers per active direction on the non-splice path, kernel socket buffers on top. At hundreds of idle connections the goroutine overhead (~tens of KB each incl. buffers) is small vs socket buffers; epoll wakeups per read/write dominate CPU under bulk load. Not measured here.
findings.technical_details: Splice path avoids pooled buffers; copyWaitWithPool (ReadWaiter) avoids pre-allocating buffer until data is ready which matters for idle connections.

findings.topic: Control plane / data plane split (spec section 14)
findings.description: Mihomo already separates (a) rule/DNS decision (tunnel.handleTCPConn/handleUDPConn, hot only at connection setup) from (b) data copy (N.Relay). A true split (separate data-plane process or kernel fast path for classified DIRECT flows) is not present. For DIRECT TCP the data plane is already kernel-side via splice but still pays 2-3 syscalls + wakeups per ~0.4 MB chunk in the proxy process; handing the established flow to nftables flow offload/eBPF removes even that, but needs a safe classification contract (sets keyed by dst/src, invalidation), i.e. complexity is in the policy layer, not in Go networking.
findings.technical_details: Key control-plane output points: tunnel.go:590-623 after rule match and DIRECT dial; metadata (src, dst, rule, proxy chain) available there. Process split (control plane process + tiny dataplane helper) offers no measurable gain for TCP over splice and only memory duplication (two Go runtimes) -> not recommended.

findings.topic: UDP relay lacks pooled batch/NAT alloc reduction opportunities
findings.description: packetSender + per-NAT goroutine + queue copies mean each inbound UDP packet is allocated/pooled and handed through chan; replacing the generic socks/tproxy UDP read path with recvmmsg would need a new ReadBatch listener loop and per-packet metadata (tproxy needs IP_RECVORIGDSTADDR control messages, which ipv4.PacketConn.ReadBatch can return via OOB buffers).
findings.technical_details: Feasible with x/net ipv4.PacketConn.ReadBatch (already a dependency, v0.35.0), but only pays at >~20-50 kpps, above what typical routers push through a userspace proxy; DNS/QUIC-direct bursts are the realistic target (hypothesis).

findings.description: Go stdlib net.TCPConn.ReadFrom/WriteTo splice only when the peer is *TCPConn/*UnixConn directly (poll.Splice); mihomo wraps conns, so it does not rely on stdlib splice; sing implements its own splice with raw syscalls. Also stdlib has fallback to copy_file_range/sendfile, irrelevant here.
findings.technical_details: go:net/splice_linux.go, go:internal/poll/splice_linux.go.

findings.description: 25.12 is stable (kernel 6.12, tree here is v25.12.6, r33311), 24.10 is old stable. Package manager is chosen at build time: apk-mbedtls when CONFIG_USE_APK else opkg. 25.12 images use apk (opkg only if built with it); 24.10 uses opkg. Main is 6.18 per task brief.
findings.technical_details: openwrt.org/releases lists 25.12 stable and 24.10 old stable (page gives no kernel/pm details). include/default-packages.mk selects apk-mbedtls vs opkg by CONFIG_USE_APK. That 25.12 default is USE_APK=y and 24.10 is opkg is from release knowledge, not read from a config in this sparse tree. Kernel 6.12 for all seven targets via KERNEL_PATCHVER:=6.12.

findings.description: Typical proxy-router targets: mt7621 (MIPS 24KEc little-endian, 880 MHz, 2 cores/4 threads MT, no FPU hardware use: soft-float, 128-512 MB RAM), ath79 (MIPS 24Kc big-endian, 400-720 MHz, 64-128 MB, weak), mediatek/filogic (aarch64 Cortex-A53, 2 cores ~1.3 GHz MT7981 / 4 cores MT7986, 256 MB-1 GB), mt7622 (aarch64 A53 dual 1.35 GHz, 512 MB), ipq40xx (ARMv7 Cortex-A7 quad ~716 MHz, neon-vfpv4, 256-512 MB), qualcommax ipq807x (aarch64 A53 quad ~1.4 GHz, 512 MB-1 GB), rockchip armv8 (A53/A55/A72, 1-8 GB), x86_64.
findings.technical_details: ramips/mt7621: CPU_TYPE 24kc, CONFIG_CPU_MIPS32_R2, CONFIG_CPU_LITTLE_ENDIAN, MIPS_MT_SMP, MIPS_CPS, NET_DSA_MT7530; ramips ARCH mipsel with no 'fpu' in FEATURES (feature list: squashfs gpio). ath79 ARCH mips (big endian), CPU_TYPE 24kc. ipq40xx ARCH arm, CPU_TYPE cortex-a7, CPU_SUBTYPE neon-vfpv4, FEATURES has fpu, NR_CPUS=4. qualcommax aarch64 cortex-a53 NR_CPUS=4. filogic aarch64 cortex-a53. mediatek/Makefile ARCH arm default (mt7623 is arm). MHz and RAM figures are from vendor specs / general knowledge, not read from the tree.

findings.topic: BPF core options in generic config
findings.description: BPF=y, BPF_SYSCALL=y, BPF_JIT=y, BPF_JIT_DEFAULT_ON=y, BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON unset, BPF_UNPRIV_DEFAULT_OFF=y, BPF_STREAM_PARSER unset, NET_SOCK_MSG=y, DEBUG_INFO and DEBUG_INFO_BTF unset, XDP_SOCKETS unset.
findings.technical_details: Consequence: bpf() syscall exists, JIT is on by default, but CO-RE/BTF-dependent loaders (cilium/ebpf with kernel BTF, vmlinux BTF for fentry/kprobes) cannot rely on /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux; programs must be pre-compiled with no CO-RE relocations against kernel types or ship their own BTF. No AF_XDP. Per-target configs add nothing BPF-related except mediatek/mt7629 NETFILTER_BPF_LINK=y. Image builders can enable KERNEL_* options in menuconfig (config/Config-kernel.in is not in the sparse tree, so exact menuconfig symbol names such as KERNEL_DEBUG_INFO_BTF/KERNEL_BPF_EVENTS/KERNEL_CGROUPS are unverified).
findings.opus_note: openwrt:target/linux/generic/config-6.12 lines 713-719: BPF_JIT=y, BPF_SYSCALL=y, BPF_STREAM_PARSER unset, JIT_ALWAYS_ON unset

findings.description: CGROUPS, KPROBES, FTRACE, PERF_EVENTS are all unset in generic config, therefore CGROUP_BPF (cgroup sock_addr/connect hooks, SO_MARK by cgroup), BPF_STREAM_PARSER (depends on CGROUP_BPF) and BPF_EVENTS (needs tracing) are not available by default.
findings.technical_details: linux net/Kconfig:354-360 BPF_STREAM_PARSER depends on CGROUP_BPF. NET_SOCK_MSG=y is set but sockmap/sk_msg redirect between sockets needs BPF_SYSCALL plus sockmap which in 6.12 does not require CGROUP_BPF for sk_msg-only use (hypothesis; sockmap needs BPF_STREAM_PARSER only for the legacy stream parser, skb verdict does not). cgroup-based socket marking for per-process routing is therefore not available without a custom kernel.
findings.opus_note: CGROUPS unset is correct (config-6.12:882), but sockmap sk_skb verdict and sk_msg do NOT need cgroups/stream parser: NET_SOCK_MSG=y (config-6.12:4230).

findings.description: 6.12 provides an eBPF JIT on MIPS (32-bit via bpf_jit_comp32.c and 64-bit), ARM 32-bit (bpf_jit_32.c, not big-endian BE32 or v3), arm64, riscv (MMU) and x86. So all common OpenWrt targets JIT. JIT_ALWAYS_ON is unset so the interpreter remains reachable only if JIT is disabled via sysctl.
findings.technical_details: arch/mips/Kconfig:70 'select HAVE_EBPF_JIT if !CPU_MICROMIPS'; arch/mips/net/Makefile builds bpf_jit_comp32.o for 32-bit, comp64 for 64-bit; arch/arm/Kconfig:96; arch/arm64/Kconfig:196; arch/riscv/Kconfig:149. ath79 big-endian MIPS32 is supported by the same JIT (not micromips). 32-bit JITs emulate 64-bit BPF registers with pairs, so 64-bit-heavy BPF programs are slower on mt7621/ipq40xx than on arm64 (hypothesis, no measurement).

findings.description: cls_bpf/act_bpf are not built in: NET_CLS_BPF, NET_ACT_BPF, NET_CLS_ACT, NET_SCH_INGRESS are unset in generic and enabled by kmod-sched-bpf / kmod-sched-core (modules) only when a package pulls them. tc is needed (package tc-bpf/tc-full).
findings.technical_details: generic config 4082,4101,4103,4214 unset. netsupport.mk KernelPackage/sched-bpf (797-809) KCONFIG NET_CLS_BPF NET_ACT_BPF, files cls_bpf.ko act_bpf.ko. sched-core sets NET_CLS_ACT=y, NET_SCH_INGRESS (722-732). A tc-bpf fast path therefore requires shipping/depending on kmod-sched-bpf and kmod-sched-core; it is available in the official feed for every target, but kmod must match the exact kernel vermagic of the installed image.

findings.description: NF_TABLES, NF_FLOW_TABLE, NFT_FLOW_OFFLOAD, NFT_TPROXY, NF_TPROXY_IPV4/6, NF_CT_NETLINK, NFT_SOCKET, TUN are unset in generic config and become =m through kmod packages; fw4 installs kmod-nft-offload etc. depending on the image. Not guaranteed present on a stripped image.
findings.technical_details: kmod-nf-flow (netfilter.mk:~198-209, NF_FLOW_TABLE, NF_FLOW_TABLE_HW, depends kmod-nf-conntrack); kmod-nft-offload (1371-1384: NF_FLOW_TABLE_INET, NFT_FLOW_OFFLOAD; depends on @IPV6 +kmod-nf-flow +kmod-nft-nat); kmod-nft-tproxy (1442-1451); kmod-nf-tproxy (224-232); kmod-nf-conntrack-netlink (~1252: NF_CT_NETLINK, CONNTRACK_EVENTS=y); kmod-tun (netsupport.mk:507-519, loaded autoload prio 30). include/netfilter.mk lines 296-328 define the NFT_CORE module group. ctnetlink is what conntrack(8) and event-based invalidation need.

findings.description: All set backends (hash, bitmap, rbtree, pipapo) are compiled into nf_tables.ko in 6.12, so timeouts, dynamic sets (add/update from packet path), intervals and concatenations (pipapo) are available whenever nf_tables loads. Only the AVX2 pipapo variant is x86-only.
findings.technical_details: linux net/netfilter/Makefile:88-99 nf_tables-objs includes nft_set_hash.o nft_set_bitmap.o nft_set_rbtree.o nft_set_pipapo.o (+ _avx2 on x86). OpenWrt's NFT_CORE group includes CONFIG_NF_TABLES_SET (netfilter.mk:297, legacy symbol). Large set element RAM cost is the kernel's, not shown here. Whether 25.12 userland nft supports a given syntax depends on libnftnl/nftables package version (unverified).

findings.description: fw4 owns 'table inet fw4' (flushed and rebuilt on reload). Hooks: input/forward/output filter, prerouting filter, dstnat (nat prerouting, priority dstnat -100), srcnat (nat postrouting, srcnat 100), raw_prerouting/raw_output (raw -300), mangle_* (mangle -150, mangle_output type route). Policies and zone chains are jumped from these.
findings.technical_details: ruleset.uc: input 115-116, forward 137-138, output 157-158, prerouting 185-186, dstnat 297-298, srcnat 313-314, raw_prerouting 370-371, raw_output 386-387, mangle_prerouting 418-419, mangle_postrouting 427-428, mangle_input 443-444, mangle_output 452-453 (type route), mangle_forward 461-462. fw4 deletes/recreates the flowtable only inside its own table.

findings.description: fw4 declares 'flowtable ft { hook ingress priority 0; devices = {...}; [flags offload;] }' when flow_offloading is enabled, with devices = all physdevs of zones (or HW offload device list). The only user is one rule in the forward chain, first rule: 'meta l4proto { tcp, udp } flow offload @ft;'. Software flowtable thus covers only forwarded TCP/UDP flows in ESTABLISHED state.
findings.technical_details: ruleset.uc:16-26 flowtable, 140-141 rule placed before chain-prepend and before the ct state vmap, so it runs before any user rules on that chain. fw4.uc resolve_offload_devices 554-572. Kernel nft_flow_offload_eval (nft_flow_offload.c:308-393) skips: non-TCP/UDP, TCP not established or fin/rst, conntrack with helper, IPS_SEQ_ADJUST, IPS_NAT_CLASH, unconfirmed ct, xfrm dst; validate allows only the forward hook (nft_flow_offload.c ~395: hook_mask = 1<<NF_INET_FORWARD). Entries age by NF_FLOW_TIMEOUT and are pushed back to conntrack on timeout/FIN/RST.

findings.description: The flowtable ingress hook (netdev ingress, priority 0) runs before IP prerouting. When a packet matches an offloaded tuple, nf_flow_offload_ip_hook forwards it directly via neigh/direct xmit and returns without traversing prerouting, forward, postrouting. Any rule in another table (mangle/tproxy/mark/killswitch/leak guard) is therefore not evaluated for packets of an offloaded flow.
findings.technical_details: nf_flow_table_ip.c:414-473 (lookup 429, NF_ACCEPT on miss 431, forward 451-465). Flow is created only when the first reply-seen forwarded packet passed the forward chain, so policy that dropped/redirected earlier packets already decided. Consequence for a safe fast path: a flow must be classified DIRECT before it is offloaded, and a later policy change (node switch, rule change) must flush the flowtable entries (conntrack -D or nft delete/recreate flowtable) because the fast path will not re-evaluate. Packets of offloaded flows are also invisible to nft counters/mihomo.

findings.description: clashwrt uses its own 'table inet clashwrt' and a fw4 zone for the tun device. Its chains sit at distinct priorities around fw4's: nat_pre at dstnat-40, dns_nat dstnat-5 (comment says it must be ahead of fw4 dstnat -100... values as in the script), mangle at mangle priority (type filter prerouting), leak6 and killswitch in forward at filter-5 (before fw4 forward at filter 0), so verdicts in forward are judged before fw4's. fw4 flow offload is toggled by uci firewall.@defaults[0].flow_offloading(_hw) and reload.
findings.technical_details: clashwrt fw.sh: TABLE='inet clashwrt' L45; dns_nat 488; leak6 500; mangle 546; nat_pre 576; killswitch 793; ensure_fw4_zone 388-423; ip rule/route policy routing 598-625; setctl.sh do_offload 1019-1037. In nftables each base chain on the same hook runs in priority order and an accept in one does not stop later chains; only drop/reject is terminal. Because fw4's forward chain 'flow offload' rule is at priority filter, a clashwrt forward chain at filter-5 runs first and can drop, but cannot prevent offload of an accepted flow except by dropping/marking before. clashwrt's own table is not flushed by fw4 reload; but fw4 'flush table inet fw4' does not touch it.

findings.topic: Kernel path: plain routing and REDIRECT/DNAT
findings.description: Plain routing: ingress -> (flowtable if offloaded) -> prerouting -> forward -> postrouting -> egress; offloadable. DNAT (fw4 dstnat) rewrites the destination before routing, still forward path, offloadable as long as no helper (fw4's flow offload handles NAT flows; entries carry NAT tuples). REDIRECT to a local port makes the route local (input path), packet is delivered to a local socket: never offloadable and never goes through the forward chain.
findings.technical_details: nf_flow_table_core.c:69-71 handles IPS_SRC_NAT/IPS_DST_NAT in route tuples. nft_flow_offload is forward-hook only so locally delivered flows never get an entry. REDIRECT/TPROXY traffic costs a full IP-stack local delivery + socket copy to userspace + a second socket to the upstream (output path).

findings.description: nft 'tproxy to :port' in prerouting looks up/assigns a local socket (nf_tproxy_get_sock_v4) and sets skb->mark; with 'ip rule fwmark X table T' and 'local default dev lo' in T the packet is routed as local and delivered to the IP_TRANSPARENT socket. It is a local delivery path, not forward; conntrack entry created is not forwarded and cannot be flow-offloaded. Direct-classified connections can be excluded in prerouting (before tproxy) by an nft set match (ip daddr @set return), keeping them on the forward path where fw4 offload applies.
findings.technical_details: net/netfilter/nft_tproxy.c:21-71 (eval_v4 with socket lookups at 49,71). clashwrt fw.sh policy routing at 613-614: 'ip rule add fwmark ... table ...; ip route replace local default dev lo table ...'. First packet of a TCP connection must be matched in prerouting each time; established-socket lookup 'transparent' check avoids re-tproxy of mid-flow packets. A DIRECT bypass by IP set only works for IP-known destinations; domain-based direct needs mihomo or a DNS-fed set (setctl's bypass4_dns).

findings.description: With fwmark+policy route 'default dev tun0', the packet is routed out through the tun device, so it stays in the forward chain (FORWARD hook then postrouting) and is consumed by the tun driver's xmit into the userspace read queue. Reply path comes from userspace write -> tun_get_user -> netif_rx/ GRO, a new ingress. Offloading such a flow is theoretically possible (dst dev = tun), but untested: tun is NOARP, flowtable devices list must include it (fw4 only adds zone physdevs, clashwrt creates a zone for the tun device), and hardware offload is impossible. Marking the packets in mangle prerouting (mark -150) happens before routing; once offloaded the mark/policy decision is frozen (see F011).
findings.technical_details: clashwrt fw.sh 624-625 'ip route replace default dev tun'; ensure_fw4_zone 388-423 makes fw4 forward accept traffic to tun. tun.ko = kmod-tun. Whether nft_flow_route accepts a NOARP dst for XMIT_NEIGH is not verified. Recommendation: never include the tun device in flowtable devices.

findings.description: Typical SoC drivers (mtk_eth_soc on mt7621/filogic, ipq40xx ess-edma, qualcommax ppe/edma) use NAPI. On mt7621 with MT7530 DSA switch the CPU port is a single GMAC link (1 Gbps, or 2.5G on filogic), all LAN ports share it, and DSA tagging adds per-packet overhead; hardware offload (PPE on mediatek, flow offload to PPE via flags offload / 'flowtable hw') exists for filogic, not mt7621 software path in the same form. Routing throughput on mt7621 is limited by per-packet CPU cost (roughly one core per direction, 880 MHz in-order MIPS, small caches), not memcpy bandwidth, so flowtable software offload helps by skipping hooks/conntrack but local-socket proxying costs many times more per packet.
findings.technical_details: ramips/mt7621/config-6.12 shows NET_DSA=y, NET_DSA_MT7530, NR_CPUS=4 with MIPS_MT. Generic NET_DSA unset (generic 4114). GRO/GSO are default in the networking core; GRO on routing path merges only local-delivery-bound or forwarded-GRO-enabled flows (forwarding via GRO needs ethtool -K gro on and may be re-segmented by GSO on egress). Concrete Mbit/s numbers are not given because none were measured here; mt7621 software NAT is commonly cited in the OpenWrt community at roughly 400-900 Mbit/s with flow offload, but this is secondary and unverified.

findings.topic: Soft-float and FPU matter for Go
findings.description: mt7621 and ath79 (MIPS 24K/24KEc) have no FPU; OpenWrt builds mipsel_24kc/mips_24kc as soft-float. Go must be built with GOMIPS=softfloat for these, otherwise the binary uses FPU instructions and crashes with SIGILL. ARMv7 ipq40xx has VFPv4+NEON (GOARM=7 ok); arm64 and x86_64 need nothing.
findings.technical_details: openwrt rules.mk:258-266 sets -msoft-float for CONFIG_SOFT_FLOAT=y; ramips FEATURES lack 'fpu' while ipq40xx/qualcommax/rockchip/mediatek list fpu. Go: GOOS=linux GOARCH=mipsle GOMIPS=softfloat for mt7621 (mipsel_24kc), GOARCH=mips GOMIPS=softfloat for ath79 big-endian, GOARCH=arm GOARM=7 for ipq40xx/mt7623, GOARCH=arm64 for filogic/ipq807x/rockchip/mt7622. GOMIPS semantics from Go docs (cmd/go), unverified against /usr/lib/go in this pass.

findings.topic: Where the proxy binary lives and RAM
findings.description: A binary in /usr/bin on a squashfs+overlay rootfs is file-backed: text pages are demand-paged from flash through the page cache and can be evicted under pressure, so RSS counts only touched pages and the kernel can reclaim them. Putting the binary in /tmp (tmpfs) pins the whole file in RAM as shmem, permanently (until deleted), and the mapped copy shares those pages; i.e. a 16 MB binary costs 16 MB of RAM regardless of use. Flash-resident execution costs flash read latency on first touch/after eviction (squashfs xz decompression CPU), which on a 128 MB router is usually preferable to pinning. Overlay (jffs2/ubifs) files are also page-cache-backed but compressed on flash, extra decompress cost.
findings.technical_details: Kernel semantics: file-backed MAP_PRIVATE text is clean and reclaimable; tmpfs pages are anonymous-like shmem, counted in Shmem and only reclaimable via swap. No swap by default: CONFIG_SWAP=y but CONFIG_ZRAM unset in generic (7795); zram comes from kmod-zram (other.mk:714) plus zram-swap package; so on stock images the whole of anonymous memory including Go heap is unreclaimable. Downloads of geo databases to /tmp also consume RAM. Recommendation: install the core in /usr/bin (or overlay for updates), keep only runtime data in /tmp, and keep Go heap small (GOGC/GOMEMLIMIT).

findings.description: OpenWrt uses musl as its libc (uClibc/uClibc-ng is obsolete and no longer offered in current releases; the rules.mk still carries LIBC-variable handling but USE_MUSL is the default). A Go program built with CGO_ENABLED=0 is statically linked, uses raw syscalls, is libc independent and runs on any OpenWrt target regardless of musl version. With CGO enabled you need the OpenWrt cross toolchain (musl) and must link to its libc; do not use host glibc.
findings.technical_details: openwrt:rules.mk:157-172 (LIBC variable, CONFIG_USE_MUSL used for BIN_DIR naming). Go net resolver with CGO_ENABLED=0 uses its pure-Go resolver (reads /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts); musl getaddrinfo not involved. Go does not use the vDSO issue-free on mips? (not verified). OpenWrt ARCH_PACKAGES e.g. mipsel_24kc, mips_24kc, arm_cortex-a7_neon-vfpv4, aarch64_cortex-a53, x86_64 (include/target.mk:368).

findings.description: OpenWrt builds C packages with PIE by default (PKG_ASLR_PIE ?= 1) when CONFIG_PKG_ASLR_PIE_ALL/REGULAR is set; this is a package-build default and imposes nothing on a prebuilt static Go binary. Go on linux/mips* uses non-PIE static exe by default (-buildmode=exe); ASLR is not required for the binary to run. PIE with CGO_ENABLED=0 on mips is supported only for some arches; not recommended since it adds relocation cost and RAM (dirty relocation pages) on 32-bit routers.
findings.technical_details: openwrt:include/hardening.mk:6-28. Static non-PIE Go exe maps text file-backed read-only with no relocation pages -> smaller RSS than PIE (hypothesis, not measured).

findings.topic: What a stock kernel lets an eBPF fast path rely on
findings.description: Without a custom kernel: bpf() + maps + JIT, tc-bpf via kmod-sched-bpf, nft sockets and sets, flowtable via kmod-nft-offload. Not available: kernel BTF/CO-RE, cgroup BPF, XDP sockets, kprobes/tracepoint BPF. An eBPF program that marks/redirects DIRECT flows at tc ingress would have to run before conntrack/nft and could skip netfilter entirely (bpf_redirect / bpf_fib_lookup), which duplicates the flowtable logic with more risk. nft + flowtable gives the same effect with kernel-maintained state and fw4 compatibility.
findings.technical_details: Combines F003-F008. XDP generic/native with native driver support exists for mtk_eth_soc and others but is not covered here (driver configs not read). bpf_fib_lookup and bpf_skb_get_xfrm_state are in 6.12 (linux net/core/filter.c) but not verified in this pass.

findings.topic: Rust platform tiers for router targets
findings.description: As of 2026-11-01 mips-unknown-linux-musl and mipsel-unknown-linux-musl are Tier 3. armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf is Tier 2 without host tools; aarch64, riscv64gc and x86_64 linux-musl are Tier 2 with host tools.
findings.technical_details: Tier 3 = no official prebuilt std and no CI guarantee; needs nightly -Zbuild-std (or rust-src) to build std for the target. Tier 2 without host tools = rust-std is shipped, but rustc/cargo do not run on that target (cross-compile only, which is all we need). The page lists musl 1.2.5 for these targets.

findings.description: OpenWrt packages feeds lang/rust (rustc 1.96.0 at master) builds the compiler from source on the build host and supports aarch64, arm, i386, loongarch64, mips, mips64, mips64el, mipsel, powerpc, riscv64, x86_64; ARM v7 maps to armv7 target, v5/v6 fall back to armv5te; mips64 uses a dedicated openwrt target.
findings.technical_details: This means Rust-in-package for MIPS is possible inside an OpenWrt buildroot (x.py dist rustc rust-std). It is the only supported MIPS path and makes the build long and heavy; it is not a prebuilt-toolchain flow. Building standalone via cargo needs nightly -Zbuild-std for mips musl.

findings.description: Linking a Rust staticlib into the Go binary needs CGO_ENABLED=1, a musl cross C toolchain per target (OpenWrt SDK) and a Rust target per arch; the fork's Makefile builds with CGO_ENABLED=0 so the pure-Go static cross-compile matrix would be lost for any profile using it.
findings.technical_details: Fork Makefile:15 uses CGO_ENABLED=0; build.yml only sets CGO_ENABLED=1 in one special job (line ~217). Each cgo call goes through runtime.cgocall -> entersyscall -> asmcgocall on the g0 stack (go:runtime/cgocall.go header comment) and pins the goroutine to an OS thread for the call duration; blocking Rust calls consume extra Ms. Go GC headroom, goroutine stacks and the scheduler remain unchanged for all remaining Go code, so the RSS floor is not lowered, only the Rust part's own allocations differ.

findings.description: I did not obtain a primary-source cgo benchmark. Commonly quoted figures are roughly tens to ~200 ns per call on x86; weaker MIPS/ARM cores are expected several times slower.
findings.technical_details: No number is cited as fact. Per-call cost matters only for fine-grained calls (per-packet rule match); batch APIs (match a whole list, or a single long-running Rust loop) amortise it. Would need a microbenchmark on real MIPS/ARM (qemu-user is not representative).

findings.description: A helper process costs its own RSS plus IPC; Rust static musl binaries are small but a tokio-based process realistically adds several MB RSS.
findings.technical_details: meow-rs, a full Rust core with REALITY/Hysteria2, reports 9.7 MB idle RSS and 7.8 MB stripped (aarch64 Apple M4, macOS, loopback), i.e. an upper-bound for a sizeable helper; a tiny non-async splice/DNS helper could be 1-2 MB (hypothesis). IPC (unix socket) per connection decision adds latency of a syscall round trip; failure handling needs a supervisor, fallback to Go path, and state sync (rules, fake-ip table) on every reload. The relay hot path cannot be handed over without passing fds (SCM_RIGHTS), which is feasible for splice-style DIRECT relay.

findings.topic: Fast DIRECT relay already in Go stdlib
findings.description: Go's net package already uses splice(2)/sendfile for TCP-to-TCP io.Copy (net/splice_linux.go), so the DIRECT TCP data plane that a Rust helper would replace is already zero-copy in kernel when both ends are *net.TCPConn.
findings.technical_details: Rust would gain nothing on bytes moved; gains only in goroutine/stack overhead per connection (about 2-8 KB stacks per goroutine, 2 goroutines per conn - hypothesis) and GC scanning.

findings.topic: Crypto asm coverage in Go on router arches
findings.description: Go stdlib has hardware-assisted AES-GCM only for arm64 (and amd64/s390x/ppc64) in crypto/internal/fips140/aes; chacha20 asm exists for arm64/ppc64x/s390x only. ARMv7 and MIPS fall back to generic Go code.
findings.technical_details: Directory listing of go:crypto/internal/fips140/aes shows aes_arm64.s, gcm_arm64.s, ctr_arm64.s; x/crypto chacha20 has chacha_arm64.s, ppc64x, s390x, no arm32 or mips. So on MIPS/ARMv7 Go is already in software-only mode.

findings.description: RustCrypto chacha20 has SIMD backends only for x86 (SSE2/AVX2/AVX512) and aarch64 NEON; everything else (MIPS, ARMv7) uses the soft backend. aes-gcm uses hardware instructions (AES-NI/CLMUL, ARMv8 crypto) or constant-time soft code elsewhere. ring/aws-lc-rs ship asm for x86_64, aarch64 and ARMv7 NEON, but I could not confirm MIPS asm; ring README warns about unusual targets.
findings.technical_details: Conclusion hypothesis: on MIPS the best Rust crypto is a portable scalar implementation, comparable to Go's generic code (rustc/LLVM may schedule a bit better; no source of benchmark). On ARMv7 ring/aws-lc may beat Go (NEON asm vs Go generic) - unmeasured. Therefore 'Rust for speed' does not fix the main CPU cost (encryption) on MIPS.

findings.topic: Rule matching already succinct in the fork
findings.description: mihomo domain/IP matching uses compact structures: component/trie (domain.go, domain_set.go succinct set, domain_map, ipcidr_trie) and binary .mrs loaders (domain_set_bin.go, ipcidr_set_bin.go). A Rust rewrite would give a small constant gain at best.
findings.technical_details: Memory of rule sets is dominated by data size (number of domains/CIDRs), which is the same in any language; gains would come from layout (already succinct) not language. CPU per lookup is microseconds; not the bottleneck at router connection rates.

findings.description: sing-tun system stack passes packets via the kernel TCP (system) or gVisor netstack (with_gvisor tag, heavy in RAM and binary size: Makefile builds with -tags with_gvisor). A Rust smoltcp/lwIP-like userspace stack would reduce RAM versus gVisor but the 'system' stack already has near-zero stack memory.
findings.technical_details: Replacing gVisor with a Rust userspace stack means cgo+FFI per packet or a helper process owning the TUN fd; high effort, still needs full parity (IPv6, UDP, ICMP). On routers the better option is nft redirect/tproxy and avoiding TUN at all. Hypothesis, no benchmark.

findings.description: meow-rs (madeye) is an active Rust reimplementation of mihomo: v0.28.0 on 2026-10-30, pushed 2026-10-30, 612 stars. Supports VLESS with REALITY and XTLS Vision, Trojan, Shadowsocks, Hysteria2 (QUIC via quiche), fake-ip DNS, rule providers; no VMess, TUIC, Hysteria v1, WireGuard, SSH, SOCKS5/HTTP outbound in its own 2026-04 gap analysis (archived, partly outdated); no in-process TUN on Linux (tproxy only), Wintun on Windows.
findings.technical_details: Own docs state TUN excluded as non-goal. .mrs rule-provider support not confirmed. Single maintainer-style project; version below 1.0.

findings.description: Official OpenWrt ipk/apk packages are published only for aarch64 (generic, cortex-a53/a72/a76) and x86_64; 32-bit arm and MIPS packages are NOT published because boring-sys (BoringSSL) does not build there. A --no-default-features --features full build exists for them, self-built.
findings.technical_details: This excludes the MIPS/ARMv7 routers that are this project's core audience.

findings.description: meow-rs v0.21.2 vs Go mihomo v1.19.31: stripped 7.8 MB vs 54.0 MB, RSS idle 9.7 MB vs 31.3 MB, peak 12.2 vs 42.4 MB, DNS QPS +43%, TCP throughput about equal.
findings.technical_details: Measured by the project on an Apple M4 Pro arm64 macOS, loopback, direct mode: not an OpenWrt router; the Go binary is a 54 MB desktop build (not a stripped/tuned fork build with GOGC/memory limit tuning). Throughput parity suggests the data plane is kernel-bound, as expected.

findings.description: Watfaq/clash-rs: release tag 'latest' on 2026-10-29, active but only 5 stars (displayed); Clash-compatible Rust core. Feature parity with mihomo (REALITY, .mrs, fake-ip, TUN) not verified here.
findings.technical_details: Its TUN uses a Rust userspace stack (smoltcp-style) in the upstream code, not confirmed this session. Rolling 'latest' tag, no semver.

findings.description: shadowsocks-rust v1.25.0 (2026-08-26), 10.9k stars, pushes in Oct 2026: very mature SS/AEAD-2022 implementation with local/redir/tun/dns modes; it is a proxy, not a Clash-config core (no rules engine like mihomo, no VLESS/Reality).
findings.technical_details: Could serve as an alternative SS data plane or reference for splice/zero-copy, but cannot replace mihomo's multi-protocol core.

findings.description: eycorsican/leaf v0.14.2 (2026-02-25), 2.8k stars, last push 2026-09-30: lightweight Rust proxy framework (SS, Trojan, VMess, VLESS?, TUN via netstack-lwip). Slower release cadence; feature parity with mihomo rules/providers is partial.
findings.technical_details: Uses lwIP via FFI for TUN, i.e. C code inside the Rust process. MIPS builds of leaf are reported in the community (unverified).

findings.topic: Cost of a full Rust core for a fork
findings.description: Option c abandons the rebase-friendly fork model: all mihomo protocol, rule, provider, API semantics would be re-implemented and tracked against upstream indefinitely.
findings.technical_details: The Go fork gets upstream protocol fixes by rebase. A Rust core must chase ~30 protocols/transports; even meow-rs, a funded active project, lacks several after seven months.

findings.topic: Where Rust RAM saving actually comes from
findings.description: The large RAM delta in meow-rs numbers (31 MB -> 9.7 MB idle) comes mostly from no GC heap headroom, no goroutine stacks and smaller binaries, i.e. things achievable only by replacing the whole runtime, not by swapping one component.
findings.technical_details: A component in cgo/helper form leaves the Go runtime (GC, ~hundreds of KB per runtime thread structures, goroutine stacks) as is. Go-side tuning (GOGC, GOMEMLIMIT, fewer goroutines, build tags) is the cheaper way to get a share of this. Other agents' areas.

findings.description: Xerj node rc.100 is running with API-key auth; MCP tools (xerj_search, xerj_map, xerj_hub_find, xerj_hub_ask, xerj_code_search, memory/brain tools) are available.
findings.technical_details: Process /usr/bin/xerj --data-dir ~/xerj-data; listeners 9200 (ES API), 8080/8081; key in ~/xerj-data/admin.key. CLI: xerj autoindex/search/code/hub/brain/feedback.

findings.description: No hub corpus covers the project's core topics. hub_find for mihomo/clash, kernel networking/nf_flowtable/conntrack, eBPF/XDP/cilium, Go runtime GC, OpenWrt, sing-tun/gvisor, nftables/TPROXY returned no_coverage or unrelated corpora.
findings.technical_details: Catalogue 7 days old at test time, no packs cached. Adjacent corpora only: golang-x-crypto (BSD-3), coroot (eBPF observability, Apache-2.0), boringtun (WireGuard data plane, BSD-3), coredns, dnscrypt-proxy (ISC), aioquic.

findings.description: Autoindex built 8 searchable indices quickly; definition-first search returns the defining file and line (e.g. ParseProxy -> fork:adapter/parser.go:11).
findings.technical_details: mlw-fork: fork (mihomo v1.19.33) (981 code files, 12133 records); mlw-deps: sing-tun, sing, gvisor, quic-go, sing-*, nftables, utls, bart (1920 code files, 76247 records); mlw-goruntime: Go 1.27.3 runtime, net, internal/poll, syscall (1721 code files, 92131 records); mlw-kernel: Linux 6.12.112 net/bpf/arch-jit/mediatek subset (1952 code files, 166826 records); mlw-openwrt: OpenWrt v25.12.6 sparse (generic config, kmods, targets) (6 code files, 870 records); mlw-fw4: firewall4 (1 code files, 473 records); mlw-ebpf: cilium/ebpf (473 code files, 6966 records); mlw-singbox: sing-box (kTLS, auto-redirect reference) (1254 code files, 17016 records). Flags used: --no-semantic --code-analyzer code; deps/goruntime via symlink farms need --follow-symlinks --follow-symlinks-outside-root (without --follow-symlinks the run exits 2).

findings.description: The pre-existing mihomo-docs index (2026-10-31) points at a deleted scratch checkout; it should be retired after the user agrees (not deleted by the agent).
findings.technical_details: xerj_map shows mihomo-docs 12119 records from run-20261031T175017Z; source folder gone.

findings.description: Lexical (BM25) code search is strong for identifiers; there is no semantic understanding with the default lexical embeddings, so conceptual questions still need grep + reading. OpenWrt Makefile/config files index as few 'code' files (6 of 116).
findings.technical_details: Default --embed-mode lexical; neural mode would need a restart of the node with a 90 MB model.
